(mechanic-embodying), the contraception / family-planning / services node (Thread F · Sexual &
Reproductive Health). "Your choices, your information, free of pressure in any direction." 84 researched,
India-grounded, COMPREHENSIVE-BUT-NEVER-EXPLICIT scenarios across the full-picture → if-when-whether →
decide-it → access-and-rights → talk-it-through → my-future-no-pressure arc, each encoded as one of the
shared v2 play actions (branch / strike-rewrite / reflect / sort / role-play / spot / match): no binary
"tap the right card". Lead mechanics: branch (decide it ×18), strike-rewrite (bust the myth ×16), sort
(real vs myth ×13). Teaches: methods/effectiveness/access (the full picture), if-when-whether it's your
call, values-based decisions, real access & rights, talking to a partner/doctor, and a future on your
terms. AUTONOMY-FIRST, mature, matter-of-fact: NO PRESSURE IN ANY DIRECTION, delaying / not having sex is
fully valid, respected, and the only 100%-certain option; being active isn't irresponsible: what matters
is informed, consensual, protected. India: RKSK / Adolescent-Friendly Health Clinics (Ujala), CONFIDENTIAL

matter: routes to a doctor / trusted adult / Childline 1098. Builds on g22 (Plan It); links g30/g31.

title: My Choices, My Future
greet: It's Lensy. 🧭 This is about YOUR choices: the honest picture on contraception, no pressure either way. Waiting is fully valid; whatever you choose is yours.

badge.title: My Choices, My Future! 🌟
badge.blurb: You know contraception and planning, can decide by your values with no pressure, and know your rights, where to find care and what stays private. Your future. 🌟

helpLine: A doctor or Adolescent-Friendly Health Clinic can answer questions and explain what stays private. If anyone pressures or exploits you, call Childline 1098.
reassure: Your choices are yours, no pressure, and waiting is valid. If anyone exploits or pressures you, it's never your fault: tell a trusted adult or Childline 1098.

scenarios.hook: Sort by real-life effectiveness: very high, or depends on perfect use?
scenarios.relearn: LARC and delaying are most certain; the pill, condoms and withdrawal depend on consistent, correct use.

scenarios.hook: Sort: protects against STIs too, or only against pregnancy?
scenarios.relearn: Only condoms protect against STIs as well as pregnancy; that's 'dual protection'.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a real contraceptive method, or a myth?
scenarios.relearn: Implants, IUDs and condoms are real methods; 'pulling out', 'washing after' and 'safe day' are unreliable myths.

scenarios.hook: Match the method to its key feature.
scenarios.relearn: Each method has a feature: LARC lasts, condoms protect from STIs, the pill is daily, EC is backup, delaying is certain.

scenarios.hook: Match the method to its real-life effectiveness.
scenarios.relearn: LARC is over 99%; the pill and condoms are lower in typical use, but still effective when used well.

scenarios.hook: Match the situation to the method worth knowing.
scenarios.relearn: Match the method to the need: dual protection, set-and-forget, backup, or certainty.

scenarios.hook: "The pill protects you against STIs."

myth.un: The pill protects you against STIs.
myth.re: The pill prevents pregnancy only; condoms are what protect against STIs.
myth.why: Different methods do different jobs.

scenarios.relearn: The pill stops pregnancy, not STIs; only condoms do both.

scenarios.hook: "Using contraception now makes you infertile later."

myth.un: Contraception now makes you infertile later.
myth.re: These methods are reversible; fertility returns after stopping.
myth.why: They prevent pregnancy while used, not permanently.

scenarios.relearn: Contraception is reversible; it doesn't cause future infertility.

scenarios.hook: "Emergency contraception is the same as an abortion."

myth.un: Emergency contraception is the same as an abortion.
myth.re: It mainly delays ovulation to prevent pregnancy; it won't end an existing pregnancy.
myth.why: It's prevention after unprotected sex, not termination.

scenarios.relearn: Emergency contraception prevents pregnancy; it is not an abortion.

scenarios.hook: "Condoms never really work, so why bother."

myth.un: Condoms don't really work.
myth.re: Used correctly every time they're about 98% effective, and they're the only STI protection.
myth.why: Most 'failure' is inconsistent or incorrect use.

scenarios.relearn: Used right every time, condoms work well and uniquely guard against STIs.

scenarios.hook: Match the term to what it means.
scenarios.relearn: Real-life effectiveness depends on consistent, correct use. That's 'typical use'.

scenarios.hook: Sort: raises real-life effectiveness, or lowers it?

items.text: Using it correctly every single time

scenarios.relearn: Consistent, correct, informed use is what makes a method actually effective.

scenarios.hook: Sort: where you can actually get these.

items.text: An IUD fitted by a clinician
Pills via a doctor / AFHC clinic
A reliable method from a rumour
The emergency pill at a pharmacy

scenarios.relearn: Pharmacies, clinics and doctors are real sources; rumours and home tricks aren't.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: with the full picture, the choice of method is genuinely yours. Feel that?
scenarios.affirm: Complete information is exactly what makes a choice truly your own.
scenarios.relearn: Full, accurate information is what makes the choice genuinely yours.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two myths in this 'advice'.

scene.text: "You can't get pregnant the first time"
"Condoms also protect from STIs"
"A certain day of the month is always safe"
"The pill is reversible"
"LARC needs nothing daily"

scenarios.why: 'First time' and 'always safe day' are myths; the other three lines are true.
scenarios.relearn: Spot the classic myths; trust evidence, not rumour.

scenarios.hook: "Only people who have a lot of sex need to think about contraception."

myth.un: Only people having lots of sex need contraception.
myth.re: Any unprotected sex can lead to pregnancy or an STI; and delaying is the certain option.
myth.why: It's about whether, not how often.

scenarios.relearn: It's the act, not the frequency; informed choice (including delaying) is for everyone.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: whether to have children, and when, is genuinely your own choice. Sit with that.
scenarios.affirm: Whether, when and how, those are yours to decide, on your timeline.
scenarios.relearn: Whether and when to have children is your own choice to make.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: choosing to delay sex, or not have it for now, is a fully valid, respected choice. Agree?
scenarios.affirm: Delaying is wise, certain and entirely your right, no one should pressure you out of it.
scenarios.relearn: Delaying or not having sex is fully valid and the most certain choice.

scenarios.hook: "A girl your age should be thinking about marriage and babies, not the future."

myth.un: At your age you should focus on marriage and babies.
myth.re: Your education and future are yours to build; family planning is a tool for the life you want.
myth.why: Whether and when is a personal right, not a deadline set by others.

scenarios.relearn: Your future is yours to plan; whether and when to marry or have children is your choice.

scenarios.hook: "Family planning is just about stopping babies."

myth.un: Family planning is only about preventing babies.
myth.re: It's a positive tool to choose if, when and how, for the life and family you want.
myth.why: Planning is about building a future, not just preventing one thing.

scenarios.relearn: Family planning is a positive tool for the future you choose.

scenarios.hook: "Spacing pregnancies doesn't really matter."

myth.un: When and how far apart you have children doesn't matter.
myth.re: Spacing supports the health of parent and child; it's part of planning.
myth.why: Timing is a real, health-relevant choice.

scenarios.relearn: If and when, including spacing, are real choices that support health.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a personal right, or something others get to force on you?

items.text: Being forced into it by others

scenarios.relearn: Whether, when, marrying and delaying are your rights; no one gets to force or shame them.

scenarios.hook: Sort: respects your choice, or pressures it?

items.text: Giving you full information and space
Pushing you to 'prove' love by having sex

scenarios.relearn: Respect gives information, space and time; pressure pushes, shames or sets deadlines.

scenarios.hook: Sort: no one should be pushed into this, versus what's yours to choose freely.
scenarios.relearn: No one should be pushed into sex, marriage or childbearing; free, informed choice is the point.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: 'no pressure in any direction' includes no pressure to wait AND no pressure to rush. Fair?
scenarios.affirm: Real freedom is the absence of pressure either way, the choice is simply yours.
scenarios.relearn: Pressure-free means neither pushed to act nor shamed for waiting.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: knowing your rights here, do you feel more in charge of your own future?
scenarios.affirm: Knowing your rights is what puts your future in your own hands.
scenarios.relearn: Knowing your reproductive rights puts your future in your hands.

scenarios.hook: Your Dadi keeps saying you should marry and start a family soon, and it's not what you want yet.

steps.prompt: At Sunday lunch, she raises it again in front of everyone. What do you do?

options.text: Snap that it's your life and none of her business
options.then: Dadi looks hurt, and your father frowns at you.

options.text: Say respectfully that the timing is your choice
options.then: The table goes quiet, and Dadi says she only wants you settled.

options.text: Make up a boyfriend so she'll finally stop
options.then: The family is thrilled, and now everyone asks to meet him.

options.text: Say you'll think about it after exams
options.then: Dadi smiles and says she'll start looking after exams, then.

steps.why: A calm, respectful 'it's my choice' holds your timeline without a fight.

steps.prompt: Later, your mother says Dadi worries because she married at seventeen. What do you think?

options.text: Maybe she's right, and I'm overthinking it
options.then: You start doubting a choice you'd made carefully.

options.text: Dadi's old-fashioned, so she doesn't count
options.then: It's easier to dismiss her, but harder to talk to her.

options.text: If Mummy agrees with her, I've already lost
options.then: You feel cornered, though your mother hasn't said that.

options.text: That explains her worry, and it's my choice
options.then: You feel kinder toward Dadi without giving up your plans.

steps.why: Understanding family worries is kind, and the decision stays yours.

steps.prompt: A cousin's wedding brings more comments about you being next. Who do you talk to afterwards?

options.text: Cousins at the wedding, over gossip
options.then: They laugh and start guessing who'll be next.

options.text: Ms. Fernandes, the school counsellor
options.then: She listens and helps you plan what to say at home.

options.text: Your followers, with a vague angry post
options.then: Relatives see it, and the comments get worse.

options.text: The aunt who started the comments
options.then: She takes it as interest and promises to find someone good.

steps.why: A trusted adult can help you hold your ground. The pressure isn't your fault.

steps.prompt: A week later, Dadi asks you gently what you want for your future. What do you say?

options.text: Say whatever will stop her worrying
options.then: She smiles, comforted, and your real plans stay unsaid.

options.text: Share your plans, and say marriage can wait
options.then: Dadi listens, then says your grandfather would have liked your plans.

options.text: That you'd rather not talk about the future
options.then: She nods sadly, and a chance to be understood passes.

options.text: Ask her to promise she'll stop pushing first
options.then: She says she can't promise to stop worrying.

steps.why: Sharing your real plans gives her a way to support you instead of worry.

scenarios.debrief: Family input is fine. The decision is still yours to make freely.
scenarios.relearn: You can respectfully hold that whether and when are your own choice.

scenarios.hook: You're not ready for sex, but your girlfriend Ananya hints that everyone your age is doing it.

steps.prompt: She says it while you're watching a film together. What goes through your mind?

options.text: Maybe I'm the odd one out
options.then: The doubt grows, though your readiness is yours alone.

options.text: If I say no, she'll think I don't like her
options.then: Worry crowds out what you actually want.

options.text: My pace is mine. 'Everyone' isn't a reason
options.then: The pressure loosens, even as she waits for an answer.

options.text: A good partner should always be ready
options.then: The idea makes your own feelings seem wrong, though they aren't.

steps.why: 'Everyone's doing it' is pressure, not a fact. Readiness is personal.

steps.prompt: Ananya asks what you're thinking. What do you say?

options.text: That your parents would never allow it
options.then: She says they'd never know, and your own reason stays unsaid.

options.text: That she's being pushy and annoying
options.then: Her face falls, and the evening goes cold.

options.text: That you like her, and you're not ready yet
options.then: She's quiet, then says she didn't mean to push.

options.text: That everyone isn't actually doing it
options.then: She lists names, and the debate becomes about other people.

steps.why: Saying both your feelings and your boundary plainly is kind and clear.

steps.prompt: A week later, Ananya hints again, and you feel worn down. Who do you talk to?

options.text: Your friend Nitin, who says you're mad to wait
options.then: He laughs it off, and your pace starts to feel like a problem.

options.text: Ananya's best friend, hoping she'll talk to her
options.then: Word gets back to Ananya, and she's hurt you went to her friend.

options.text: Your aunt Kavita, who you trust
options.then: She listens and says your pace is yours, whoever is asking.

options.text: An online forum, anonymously
options.then: The replies swing between jokes and lectures, and none of them know you.

steps.why: A trusted adult can help you hold your pace. Pressure is never your fault.

scenarios.debrief: Readiness is personal. Delaying is valid and certain, and pressure is never your fault.
scenarios.relearn: Decide by your own readiness, not 'everyone's doing it'.

scenarios.hook: "Wanting to wait means something's wrong with you."

myth.un: Wanting to wait means something's wrong with you.
myth.re: Waiting is a common, healthy, fully respected choice.
myth.why: Readiness differs for everyone, and that's normal.

scenarios.relearn: Choosing to wait is normal, healthy and respected.

scenarios.hook: You want to decide for yourself whether, and when, you're ready for a sexual relationship.

steps.prompt: You're not sure where to begin. What do you do first?

options.text: See what your friends say they're doing
options.then: Their stories are mostly bragging, and you can't tell what's true.

options.text: Get the facts from a doctor or reliable source
options.then: You learn the real picture, from protection to the option of waiting.

options.text: Wait for your partner to raise it
options.then: Weeks pass, and the decision drifts toward someone else's timing.

options.text: Go with whatever feels right in the moment
options.then: You decide to play it by ear, and the facts never get gathered.

steps.why: Accurate facts are the base of any sound decision.

steps.prompt: A few days later, you list what matters to you. What goes at the top?

options.text: Not seeming immature to my friends
options.then: The list starts to look like it's about them, not you.

options.text: Keeping my partner happy
options.then: You notice the list is mostly about someone else.

options.text: What my parents would say if they knew
options.then: Their voices fill the page, and your own gets quieter.

options.text: My own readiness, health and future plans
options.then: Writing it down, your own priorities come into focus.

steps.why: Your own values, not others' expectations, are the compass.

steps.prompt: Your partner says everyone your age is already doing it. What do you do?

options.text: Wonder if you're somehow behind everyone else
options.then: The doubt grows, though the claim isn't true.

options.text: Call it a myth, and say you'll take your time
options.then: Your partner pauses. "Okay. I didn't mean to push."

options.text: Argue that they're the one being immature
options.then: The talk turns into a fight about who's more grown-up.

options.text: Ask your friends to settle whether it's true
options.then: Your friends give five different answers, all of them guesses.

steps.why: Not everyone is doing it, and a real choice is never rushed. Being pressured is never your fault.

steps.prompt: You want an older person's view without being told what to do. Who do you ask?

options.text: An older cousin who brags about his experience
options.then: He tells stories that are more about him than about you.

options.text: A forum where strangers vote on your choice
options.then: Strangers vote, and the result feels random and loud.

options.text: A trusted adult or counsellor who listens first
options.then: She listens, shares a few facts, and leaves the choice with you.

options.text: No one. It's simpler to decide fast
options.then: You decide quickly, then keep second-guessing it.

steps.why: A trusted adult can support your thinking without deciding for you.

steps.prompt: You've made your choice. A week later, someone questions it. What do you do?

options.text: Change it, just to make the questions stop
options.then: The questions stop, but the choice no longer feels like yours.

options.text: Explain yourself again and again until they agree
options.then: They never quite agree, and you feel worn out.

options.text: Hide it, and pretend you never decided anything
options.then: Pretending takes more energy than the choice ever did.

options.text: Stand by it, and know you can revisit it later
options.then: You feel steady. The choice is yours, and so is the right to change it.

steps.why: Owning a choice means holding it, and changing it only for your own reasons.

scenarios.debrief: Consent, safety and the law come first. Then gather facts, weigh your values, choose without rushing, and own it.
scenarios.relearn: Decide by facts and your own values, freely, and own it.

scenarios.hook: If you and Meera ever decide to have sex, you both want to avoid pregnancy and STIs.

steps.prompt: Meera says the pill would cover everything. What do you say?

options.text: Agree, since the pill is very effective
options.then: You both feel covered, though STIs aren't covered at all.

options.text: That condoms ruin trust, so the pill is better
options.then: Meera frowns. "Why would protecting each other ruin trust?"

options.text: That only condoms also protect against STIs
options.then: Meera looks surprised. "I didn't know that. So both?"

options.text: That you'll leave it all to her to sort out
options.then: Meera goes quiet. "So it's just my job?"

steps.why: The pill prevents pregnancy only. Condoms are the one method that also protects against STIs.

steps.prompt: Later, Meera asks where you'd even get reliable advice. What do you suggest?

options.text: A friend's older brother who 'knows things'
options.then: His advice is half jokes and half wrong.

options.text: A doctor or adolescent-friendly clinic
options.then: The clinic explains dual protection clearly and privately.

options.text: Videos online, since no one will know
options.then: Some videos are useful, and many are selling something.

options.text: Each of you asks your own friends
options.then: You come back with two different stories.

steps.why: A doctor or adolescent-friendly clinic gives accurate, confidential advice.

steps.prompt: A friend says condoms 'don't really work', so why bother. What do you think?

options.text: Maybe he's right, and it's not worth it
options.then: The doubt sticks, and the plan feels shakier.

options.text: Then the pill alone will have to do
options.then: That leaves STIs uncovered, though it feels like a plan.

options.text: I'll ask him for proof and argue it out
options.then: The argument goes nowhere, and neither of you changes your mind.

options.text: Used correctly every time, they work well
options.then: You know the facts, and the myth loses its grip.

steps.why: Used correctly every time, condoms work well, and only they also protect against STIs.

scenarios.debrief: For both pregnancy and STIs, condoms are essential, with another method optional for extra cover.
scenarios.relearn: Want both kinds of protection? Condoms are the dual-protection move.

scenarios.hook: A condom split last night, and you're worried about pregnancy.

steps.prompt: It's morning and you have school. What do you do?

options.text: Hope for the best and wait it out
options.then: Each day the worry grows, and the window gets shorter.

options.text: Ask a pharmacist about emergency contraception
options.then: The pharmacist explains it works best soon, within five days.

options.text: Search online for home remedies
options.then: The remedies are myths, and the morning slips away.

options.text: Wait until the weekend, when it's easier to go
options.then: By Saturday, three days have passed.

steps.why: Emergency contraception works best soon after, within five days.

steps.prompt: Your partner texts, anxious, asking what happens now. What do you say?

options.text: That it's not their problem to worry about
options.then: They go quiet, hurt at being shut out.

options.text: That it's probably fine, so don't stress
options.then: They feel brushed off, and you both stay uneasy.

options.text: That you'll decide together, and get help today
options.then: The reply comes fast: "Okay. I'll come with you."

options.text: That it's their fault for buying cheap ones
options.then: A fight starts, and nothing gets decided.

steps.why: Facing it together, calmly, helps you both act in time.

steps.prompt: A friend warns that emergency contraception is 'like an abortion'. What do you think?

options.text: Maybe I shouldn't take it, then, just in case
options.then: You hesitate, and another day slips past.

options.text: I'll take it, though it's a kind of abortion
options.then: You take it, but carry a guilt that rests on a myth.

options.text: It isn't an abortion. A pharmacist can confirm
options.then: You check, and the pharmacist explains it simply.

options.text: I'll ask more friends what they think
options.then: Everyone has a view, and none of them are facts.

steps.why: Emergency contraception mainly delays ovulation. It is not an abortion.

steps.prompt: A few days on, you're still anxious. Who do you talk to?

options.text: No one. It'll pass on its own
options.then: The anxiety lingers, and you sleep badly.

options.text: Only your partner, and agree to never mention it again
options.then: The topic closes, but the worry stays open.

options.text: A forum full of strangers' stories
options.then: The stories make you more anxious, not less.

options.text: A doctor or clinic, with a trusted adult if you like
options.then: The doctor answers your questions, and you feel calmer.

steps.why: A doctor can answer what happens next, and support makes it easier.

scenarios.debrief: After unprotected sex or a split condom, emergency contraception within five days is the backup.
scenarios.relearn: After a slip, emergency contraception works best within 5 days.

scenarios.hook: You've forgotten your daily pill three times this month.

steps.prompt: You notice the missed pills on Sunday night. What do you do?

options.text: Keep going and hope it's fine
options.then: The next week, you miss another one.

options.text: Stop the pill altogether, since it isn't working
options.then: You're left with no method and no plan.

options.text: Book a doctor's visit to talk about other methods
options.then: The clinic gives you a slot for Tuesday.

options.text: Set five alarms and promise to try harder
options.then: The alarms work for a week, then you start snoozing them.

steps.why: If daily isn't working, a doctor can help you find a method that fits.

steps.prompt: A friend says methods like the implant cause infertility later. What do you think?

options.text: That settles it. I'll avoid them
options.then: You cross off options before learning anything about them.

options.text: That's a myth. I'll check with the doctor
options.then: The doctor confirms fertility returns after stopping.

options.text: Maybe, so I'll ask her for more stories
options.then: Her stories get scarier, but none come with facts.

options.text: I'll look it up and trust what most people say
options.then: The comments are split, and you're more confused.

steps.why: Contraception doesn't cause later infertility. These methods are reversible.

steps.prompt: At a doctor's visit, she asks what matters most to you in a method. What do you say?

options.text: Whatever my friends are using, I suppose
options.then: She asks what suits you, not them.

options.text: Whatever is cheapest. Nothing else matters
options.then: She covers costs, but you've skipped what fits your life.

options.text: Something I don't have to remember every day
options.then: She explains options like the implant and IUD, which last for years.

options.text: Just pick for me. You're the doctor
options.then: She smiles. "I'll explain, but it's your choice."

steps.why: Matching the method to your real life is what makes it work.

steps.prompt: A week later, you're weighing two options the doctor described. What helps you decide?

options.text: Picking whichever one sounds least scary to you
options.then: You pick fast, without knowing why the other might suit you better.

options.text: Asking the doctor more, then choosing
options.then: The answers make the choice clearer, and it feels like yours.

options.text: Asking your cousin which one she'd pick
options.then: She picks hers, which fits her life, not yours.

options.text: Putting the whole decision off until next year
options.then: Meanwhile, the missed pills keep happening.

steps.why: Clear facts plus your own needs make the choice yours.

scenarios.debrief: The best method is the one you'll actually use consistently.
scenarios.relearn: Match the method to your real life; a forgotten pill protects less.

scenarios.hook: You're weighing a decision about contraception and want the facts first.

steps.prompt: A forward on the family group has 'shocking facts' about it. What do you do?

options.text: Trust it, since so many people shared it
options.then: The claims slip into your thinking, unchecked.

options.text: Forward it to friends to see what they think
options.then: The message spreads further, and so does the confusion.

options.text: Delete it and decide on gut feeling
options.then: You avoid the rumour, but still have no real facts.

options.text: Check the claims with a doctor or clinic
options.then: The clinic explains which parts are true, and most aren't.

steps.why: Facts come from a doctor or clinic, not forwarded messages.

steps.prompt: A popular video says the opposite of the forward. Who do you believe?

options.text: The video, since it has millions of views
options.then: Later you notice the video ends with a product to buy.

options.text: Whichever one feels more comfortable
options.then: You pick the comforting version, true or not.

options.text: Neither, until a clinician confirms it
options.then: A quick question at the clinic settles it.

options.text: The one my friends agree with
options.then: You go with the group, not the facts.

steps.why: When sources clash, a clinician or reliable health source settles it.

steps.prompt: A friend asks where to get facts she can trust. What do you tell her?

options.text: A doctor or adolescent-friendly clinic
options.then: She asks where the nearest one is.

options.text: Whatever most people online agree on
options.then: She finds a popular post, confident and wrong.

options.text: The family WhatsApp group, since elders know
options.then: She gets three forwards and a lecture.

options.text: Trust your gut. Facts change all the time
options.then: She feels free, and no better informed.

steps.why: Reliable facts come from clinicians and trusted health sources.

scenarios.debrief: A good decision starts with accurate facts from real sources.
scenarios.relearn: Base the choice on a clinician and reliable sources, not rumour.

scenarios.hook: Mr. Reddy says people make different life choices, but a few things always hold.

steps.prompt: He asks the class which things always hold. What do you say?

options.text: Whatever your family decides
options.then: He asks, "Even if a family decision ignores someone's consent?"

options.text: Consent, safety and the law
options.then: He nods and writes all three on the board.

options.text: Anything goes, if you want it enough
options.then: He raises an eyebrow. "Even if the other person doesn't?"

options.text: Whatever most people around you do
options.then: He asks, "And if most people are mistaken?"

steps.why: Consent, safety and the law protect everyone, whatever else people choose.

steps.prompt: A classmate says, "If two people agree, age doesn't matter." What do you think?

options.text: He has a point. Agreement is what counts
options.then: Mr. Reddy pauses. "Agreement matters, but it isn't the only thing."

options.text: It's none of our business what others do

scenarios.hook: You want to agree on protection with your girlfriend Divya, long before anything happens.
scenarios.setup: You're sitting on the steps after tuition.

steps.prompt: Divya asks: "You've gone quiet. What's on your mind?"

options.text: "Nothing. It's nothing."
options.then: She nudges you. "Doesn't look like nothing. Tell me tomorrow?"

options.text: "If we ever do this, I want us to use protection. Agreed?"
options.then: Divya smiles. "I'm glad you said it first. Let me think about it tonight."

options.text: "Have you ever thought about, you know, stuff? Like, later?"
options.then: She laughs. "What stuff?" You lose your nerve.

options.text: "My friends say we should be careful, so..."
options.then: "Your friends?" she asks. "What do they have to do with us?"

steps.why: A clear, matter-of-fact line makes it easy to agree.

steps.prompt: The next day, Divya messages: "About yesterday. Can we talk about it properly?"

options.text: "Sure, but only if you bring it up first."
options.then: "Why me first?" she replies, and you both wait.

options.text: "Yes. I'd rather we agree now, while things are calm."
options.then: "That makes sense," she replies. "Better now than later."

options.text: "No reason to. Forget it ever came up."
options.then: She sends a thumbs up, and the talk slips away again.

options.text: "My cousin had a scare, so we need to talk."
options.then: "Does your cousin know you're telling me?" she replies.

steps.why: Agreeing in a calm moment, ahead of time, is what makes it work.

steps.prompt: A week later, Divya asks: "If we ever needed a plan, where would we even start?"

options.text: "We'll just figure it out when it happens."
options.then: She raises an eyebrow. "That's not much of a plan."

options.text: "You sort it out. You're better at these things."
options.then: "Why me?" she asks. "It's both of us."

options.text: "Whatever my friends use, I guess."
options.then: "Your friends aren't us," she says.

options.text: "We get the facts together, from a clinic."
options.then: Divya nods. "Okay. Together."

steps.why: Getting the facts together keeps the plan shared and accurate.

scenarios.relearn: Agreeing on protection beforehand is mature and caring.

scenarios.hook: You raise protection with your partner Rhea, and she pulls a face.
scenarios.setup: You're walking back from the bus stop.

steps.prompt: Rhea says: "Ugh, this is so unromantic. Can we not?"

options.text: "Okay, forget I said anything."
options.then: She brightens, and the topic hangs, unspoken, for days.

options.text: "Fine. I'll sort it out on my own, so you don't have to."
options.then: "On your own?" she asks. "Isn't it about both of us?"

options.text: "Looking after each other is part of caring. Let's talk."
options.then: Rhea sighs, then smiles a little. "Okay. Quickly, though."

options.text: "Unromantic? It's called being responsible."
options.then: She rolls her eyes. "Okay. Lecture over?"

steps.why: Caring includes the practical talk, and saying so kindly keeps it open.

steps.prompt: A few days later, Rhea asks: "Why does this have to be such a big conversation, anyway?"

options.text: "Because you clearly don't take it seriously."
options.then: Her face closes. "Wow. Okay."

options.text: "It doesn't. Five minutes, so we both know the plan."
options.then: "Five minutes," she says. "I can do five minutes."

options.text: "It doesn't. Let's just leave it, then."
options.then: She shrugs, relieved, but a day later she brings it back up herself.

options.text: "Because my sister says couples always mess this up."
options.then: "Your sister?" Rhea asks. "Since when is she part of this?"

steps.why: Keeping it short and simple makes the talk easy to say yes to.

steps.prompt: Later that week, Rhea asks: "So what would you even want us to agree on?"

options.text: "Whatever you think is best, honestly. I'm easy either way."
options.then: She frowns. "That's not agreeing. That's handing it to me."

options.text: "That you'll remember to sort it out."
options.then: "Why me?" she asks. "It's both of us."

options.text: "That if we ever do, we use protection and check in."
options.then: Rhea nods. "Okay. That's simple. Agreed."

options.text: "That we'll just know when the time is right."
options.then: She laughs. "That's not a plan, though."

steps.why: A clear, shared agreement is what makes the talk worth having.

scenarios.relearn: Caring includes the practical talk; a good partner will have it.

scenarios.hook: Your boyfriend Arnav has hinted that he wants to go further, and you're not ready.
scenarios.setup: He calls you that evening.

steps.prompt: Arnav asks: "So, have you thought about what I said?"

options.text: "Maybe I'm just scared. I'll get over it."
options.then: "There's nothing to be scared of," he says, and keeps pushing the point.

options.text: "I have. I'm not ready, and I need you to respect that."
options.then: There's a pause. "Okay. I hear you."

options.text: "I'm not ready. Is something wrong with me?"
options.then: "No, of course not," he says, then trails off.

options.text: "Why do you always have to push me like this, Arnav?"
options.then: "I'm not pushing," he says sharply. "I just asked."

steps.why: Saying you're not ready, and asking for respect, is clear and complete.

steps.prompt: Arnav says: "I just thought, since we've been together a year..."

options.text: "You're right. I should be ready by now."
options.then: He sounds hopeful, and you feel a deadline you didn't set.

options.text: "So you're keeping count? That's creepy."
options.then: "It's not like that," he says, hurt.

options.text: "A year doesn't decide it for me. Still not ready."
options.then: He goes quiet. "Okay. That's fair."

options.text: "I know. I'm sorry I'm such a disappointment."
options.then: "You're not," he says, but the guilt stays with you.

steps.why: Time together doesn't set your readiness. Only you do.

steps.prompt: Meenal di, your best friend's grown-up sister, asks: "You seem low. Everything okay with Arnav?"

options.text: "It's fine. All couples deal with this."
options.then: She lets it go, and you go home with it still heavy.

options.text: "I think I'm the problem. I'm just too slow for him."
options.then: "There's no such thing as too slow," she says firmly.

options.text: "He's been pushing, and I've said I'm not ready."
options.then: Meenal di nods. "You've been clear. None of this is on you."

options.text: "My friends say I should give in so I don't lose him."
options.then: "That's bad advice," she says gently. "Your no counts, whoever says otherwise."

steps.why: Telling someone you trust helps you hold your line. Pressure is never your fault.

steps.prompt: A few days later, Arnav says: "Okay. I'll wait. Just don't make me wait forever."

options.text: "Thanks for being so patient with me. I know it's hard for you."
options.then: "It is hard," he says, and your waiting starts to feel like a debt.

options.text: "Okay. I'll keep checking if I'm ready yet."
options.then: He sounds pleased, and a clock starts ticking in your head.

options.text: "There's no timeline. If that doesn't work, we'll talk."
options.then: Arnav is quiet, then says, "Okay. No timeline."

options.text: "Wow. Way to make it about you again."
options.then: "That's not fair," he says, and the call ends tense.

steps.why: Readiness has no timeline, and you never owe anyone one.

scenarios.relearn: You can say you're not ready and ask for respect, clearly.

scenarios.hook: Talking about 'if we ever', your girlfriend Kavya says she doesn't like condoms.

options.text: "Let's find a plan we're both okay with. Protection stays."

options.then: She puts the phone down. "Why is it all on me?"

options.text: "Not liking them isn't a real reason, Kavya."

steps.prompt: Kavya asks: "But isn't the pill enough on its own?"

options.text: "It prevents pregnancy, but not infections. Condoms do both."

options.text: "The pill is dangerous anyway."

options.text: "Then we wait until we do. Protection isn't optional."
options.then: Kavya nods. "Okay. That's fair. No pressure either way."

options.text: "Don't be silly. Nothing bad will happen."

options.text: "Tell them everything, so they understand."

options.text: "I'll do all the talking. You can just nod."
options.then: "Okay," she says, relieved, but she looks smaller somehow.

options.text: "That you have a question for the doctor."

options.then: "Um, I'd rather do it myself," she says.

options.text: "Only if you want to. It's your call."
options.then: She smiles. "Maybe just Neha. She's been wondering too."

steps.why: A trusted adult can speak up for you. The pressure is not your fault.

steps.prompt: Your father says the final call is yours, though he's worried. What do you do?

options.text: Turn the seat down so he won't worry
options.then: His face relaxes, and your own plans fold away quietly.

options.text: Take it, but stop telling the family anything
options.then: The move happens, and home starts to feel far away.

options.text: Ask him to decide for you after all
options.then: He hesitates, and your choice slips back into other hands.

options.text: Take the seat, and keep talking with him
options.then: He nods, and you start planning the move together.

steps.why: Owning the choice while keeping family close builds the future you want.

scenarios.debrief: Family input is fine, but the choice between college and marriage is yours.
scenarios.relearn: Family planning is a tool for the life you want; your education is yours to build.

scenarios.hook: A forward says a contraceptive method 'causes cancer', and it's scaring you off it.

steps.prompt: The forward has a scary video and thousands of shares. What do you do?

options.text: Rule the method out completely, just in case
options.then: The fear eases, and so does any real look at your options.

options.text: Forward it to your friends as a warning
options.then: Three friends panic, and one asks you what to do.

options.text: Trust it, since so many people shared it
options.then: The share count feels like proof, though it proves nothing.

options.text: Ask a doctor about the claim before deciding
options.then: You note it down to ask at the clinic next week.

steps.why: A frightening forward isn't a fact. A doctor can tell you what's true.

steps.prompt: Your aunt Shobha says a neighbour told her the same thing. What do you think?

options.text: Two people saying it makes it more likely
options.then: The rumour grows heavier, with nothing new behind it.

options.text: Hearing it twice still isn't evidence
options.then: You stay curious, but the fear loosens its grip.

options.text: She's older, so she must have checked
options.then: You trust her age over any actual facts.

options.text: I'll ask her to drop it so I can stop worrying
options.then: She stops talking about it, but the worry stays with you.

steps.why: A rumour repeated is still a rumour. Facts come from a doctor or a reliable source.

steps.prompt: Days later, a doctor at the clinic asks what's on your mind. What do you say?

options.text: Skip the rumour, since it sounds silly to ask
options.then: You leave with the fear still sitting at the back of your mind.

options.text: Ask her to promise the method is perfectly safe
options.then: She says she can explain the facts honestly, not promise perfection.

options.text: Show her the forward and ask what's true
options.then: She reads it, explains the real facts, and your fear settles.

options.text: Ask for a different method without saying why
options.then: She suggests one, but the fear never gets cleared up.

steps.why: Bringing the actual claim lets the doctor replace fear with facts.

scenarios.debrief: Fear-based rumours aren't facts. Check with a doctor, then decide.
scenarios.relearn: Decide from facts, not from a scary rumour designed to frighten you.

scenarios.hook: You'd planned a clinic visit carefully, but froze at the desk and left without asking anything.

steps.prompt: On the bus home, you replay it. What do you tell yourself?

options.text: The receptionist made it awkward, so it's on her
options.then: Blaming her feels easier, and the plan quietly fades.

options.text: It didn't go to plan, so I'll work out what to change
options.then: The sting fades, and you start thinking about next time.

options.text: Clinics just aren't for people like me
options.then: The door you'd opened starts to close.

options.text: I'm hopeless at this, so why bother
options.then: The harsh words make the next try feel even harder.

steps.why: Owning what happened, without blame, lets you adjust and try again.

steps.prompt: That evening, you think about what tripped you up. What do you change?

options.text: Write your questions down so you can read them
options.then: You fill half a page, and the questions feel less scary on paper.

options.text: Pick a time when the clinic is nearly empty
options.then: You find a quiet slot, but the words still feel stuck.

options.text: Ask a friend to go in and ask for you
options.then: Your friend agrees, but your questions would come out second-hand.

options.text: Nothing. Next time you'll simply be braver
options.then: There's no plan, just a hope that next time feels different.

steps.why: A small, practical change makes the next attempt easier.

steps.prompt: A week later, the receptionist asks why you've come in. What do you say?

options.text: That it's just a general check-up
options.then: You're booked for a general check, and your real questions may not come up.

options.text: Mumble and hope she doesn't ask again
options.then: She asks you to repeat it, and your face burns.

options.text: That you have some sexual health questions
options.then: She nods, writes it down, and asks you to take a seat.

options.text: That a friend sent you to ask for them
options.then: She looks unsure whose appointment this is.

steps.why: A plain reason gets you to the right doctor without fuss.

steps.prompt: Afterwards, a friend asks why you went back after leaving the first time. What do you say?

options.text: That the receptionist was rude the first time
options.then: Your friend frowns at the clinic, and the real story gets lost.

options.text: That someone made you go back
options.then: It sounds simpler, but it gives away a choice that was yours.

options.text: That it didn't go to plan, so you tried again
options.then: Your friend says they'd probably have given up.

options.text: That the first clinic was useless
options.then: Your friend now thinks the clinic is bad, though it wasn't.

steps.why: Owning both the stumble and the retry is what deciding well looks like.

scenarios.debrief: Deciding well includes owning the outcome and adjusting. That's the skill.
scenarios.relearn: Owning a choice includes handling the outcome calmly; that's part of deciding well.

scenarios.hook: You've decided you want a contraceptive method. Now you need to know where to get it.

steps.prompt: A site pops up selling pills with no prescription and fast delivery. What do you do?

options.text: Order it, since it's quick and private
options.then: A packet arrives with a label you can't read and no instructions.

options.text: Borrow a few from a friend who uses them
options.then: Your friend hands some over, unsure if they'd even suit you.

options.text: Find a doctor or adolescent-friendly clinic
options.then: You look up the nearest clinic and see it has youth hours.

options.text: Ask a chemist to pick something for you
options.then: He offers a strip, but can't ask the questions a doctor would.

steps.why: A doctor or clinic matches the method to you. An unverified pill online is a gamble.

steps.prompt: You worry a clinic will want a parent's permission just to talk. What do you do?

options.text: Assume it will, and drop the idea
options.then: The plan stalls for weeks on a rule you never checked.

options.text: Call the clinic and ask how it works at your age
options.then: The counsellor says it's confidential, and you can bring a trusted adult if you like.

options.text: Ask a friend to pose as your parent
options.then: The plan gets complicated, and a little risky.

options.text: Search online for what the rules are
options.then: You find five answers for five different places.

steps.why: Asking the clinic gets the real answer. It's confidential, and a trusted adult can come too.

steps.prompt: When you do see a doctor, she explains a few options and asks which fits your life. What do you do?

options.text: Pick the one your friend uses
options.then: It worked for her, but you never check whether it fits you.

options.text: Ask what each needs from you day to day
options.then: She goes through them, and one stands out as a fit for you.

options.text: Pick whichever sounds cheapest
options.then: It saves money, but you haven't asked if you'll manage it.

options.text: Ask her to choose so you don't have to
options.then: She says she'll guide you, but the choice is yours.

steps.why: Asking how each one fits your life helps you choose a method you'll actually use.

scenarios.debrief: Knowing the real route, a clinic or doctor, turns the choice into action.
scenarios.relearn: Knowing where to go is part of deciding; pick the real service, not a quick fix.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Ayesha made the opposite choice to you about dating, and says hers is the only right one.

steps.prompt: She says it at lunch, loud enough for others to hear. What do you do?

options.text: Argue until she admits she's wrong
options.then: The table goes quiet, and the friendship feels strained.

options.text: Agree with her to avoid a scene
options.then: The moment passes, and it feels like you've disowned your own choice.

options.text: Say calmly that both choices can be right
options.then: Ayesha pauses, then shrugs and says maybe.

options.text: Laugh it off and change the subject
options.then: The topic drops, but you feel judged all afternoon.

steps.why: Beyond consent, safety and the law, there's no single right choice. Both can be valid.

steps.prompt: That evening, you start wondering if she's right after all. What do you do?

options.text: Switch to her choice to end the doubt
options.then: The doubt stops, and so does the sense that this is yours.

options.text: Ask your other friends to vote on it
options.then: The vote splits down the middle and settles nothing.

options.text: Decide she's judging you, and avoid her
options.then: You miss her, and the question is still unanswered.

options.text: Check your reasons against your own values
options.then: Your reasons still hold, and the doubt quiets down.

steps.why: Your choice rests on your values, not on who argues loudest.

steps.prompt: A week later, another friend asks you which choice is better. What do you say?

options.text: That your own choice is the better one
options.then: Your friend looks uneasy, and you hear Ayesha in your own words.

options.text: That it depends on each person's values
options.then: Your friend relaxes and starts thinking it through for herself.

options.text: Whatever Ayesha says, to keep the peace
options.then: Your friend leaves with Ayesha's answer instead of her own.

options.text: That she should copy you, to be safe
options.then: She nods, but the choice isn't really hers now.

steps.why: Respecting different reasoned choices helps others decide by their own values too.

scenarios.debrief: Different reasoned choices can both be right. Yours rests on your values.
scenarios.relearn: Beyond the floor, your reasoned choice is valid even if a friend chose differently.

scenarios.hook: Relatives keep quizzing you about your plans for marriage and children, and you feel exposed.

steps.prompt: At a wedding, an aunt asks loudly when you'll settle down. What do you do?

options.text: Explain your whole plan to prove you've thought it through
options.then: She picks apart every detail, and others join in.

options.text: Make up a plan that will satisfy her
options.then: She's pleased, and soon the family repeats your made-up plan.

options.text: Tell her it's rude to ask
options.then: She looks offended, and the story spreads by evening.

options.text: Smile and say you'll decide that privately
options.then: She raises an eyebrow, then moves on to the food.

steps.why: You can keep your plans private. A kind, brief line is enough.

steps.prompt: Later, your cousin Mitali asks the same thing, sounding genuinely curious. What do you do?

options.text: Share what you're comfortable sharing, no more
options.then: Mitali listens and shares some of her own plans too.

options.text: Tell her everything, then worry it'll spread
options.then: She means well, but you lie awake wondering who else will hear.

options.text: Snap that it's nobody's business
options.then: She looks hurt, and you lose a chance to talk with someone kind.

options.text: Ask her to update the family so they stop
options.then: The family hears a version of your plans you never meant to share.

steps.why: Privacy means you choose what to share and with whom, even with people you trust.

steps.prompt: A week later, the family WhatsApp group asks everyone to share their future plans. What do you do?

options.text: Post your plans in full so they'll stop asking
options.then: Replies pile up with opinions you didn't ask for.

options.text: Leave the group in protest
options.then: Your exit becomes the chat's new topic.

options.text: Skip it, or reply with something light
options.then: A few people tease you, then the chat moves on.

options.text: Ask your parents to answer for you
options.then: They post their own version of your future.

steps.why: You don't owe anyone your plans. Keeping them private is part of the choice.

scenarios.debrief: You can decide privately. No one is owed your reproductive plans.
scenarios.relearn: You can decide privately; you don't owe everyone an explanation.

scenarios.hook: You've thought it through and want to wait to have sex, but you keep second-guessing it.

steps.prompt: A friend says waiting will make you seem boring. What goes through your mind?

options.text: Maybe I should rethink, so I don't seem boring
options.then: You start weighing how you'll look instead of what you want.

options.text: Maybe waiting means something's wrong with me
options.then: The worry grows, though nothing about waiting is a problem.

options.text: I'll pretend I'm not waiting, so no one asks
options.then: The pretending takes more energy than the choice ever did.

options.text: My reasons are mine, and waiting is valid
options.then: You feel steadier, and the word boring loses its sting.

steps.why: Waiting is a valid, respected choice, and the most certain one.

steps.prompt: Your partner Dev asks, kindly, why you want to wait. What do you do?

options.text: Say you'll change your mind soon, so he's not upset
options.then: He relaxes, and now there's a promise you didn't want to make.

options.text: Share your reasons, as much as you want to
options.then: Dev listens and says he's glad you told him.

options.text: Say it's because of your parents
options.then: Dev thinks it's their rule, and your own reasons stay hidden.

options.text: Ask what he'd prefer you to do
options.then: He hesitates, and the choice starts tipping toward his answer.

steps.why: Sharing your real reasons helps a partner understand and respect your choice.

steps.prompt: Months later, an online quiz tells you you're behind for waiting. What do you do?

options.text: Start wondering whether to catch up
options.then: The quiz plants a doubt your own reasons don't support.

options.text: Ask friends whether they're behind too
options.then: Everyone answers differently, and the comparison takes over.

options.text: Hunt for articles proving waiting is better
options.then: You find some, and notice you'd needed outside proof.

options.text: Trust your reasoned choice over a quiz
options.then: You close the tab, and your own reasons feel solid again.

steps.why: A reasoned choice to wait needs no one's approval, least of all a quiz's.

scenarios.debrief: A reasoned choice to wait is fully valid. It needs no one's approval.
scenarios.relearn: Delaying is a full, certain choice; it doesn't need anyone's approval.

scenarios.hook: Varun, an older student, threatens to share your private chats unless you agree to meet him.

steps.prompt: His latest message says you have until tonight. What goes through your mind?

options.text: It's my fault for chatting with him at all
options.then: The shame feels heavy, though the threat is his doing, not yours.

options.text: Maybe I'm overreacting. He's probably bluffing
options.then: You try to believe it, but the deadline keeps ticking in your head.

options.text: A yes forced by a threat isn't a choice
options.then: Seeing it clearly, you feel a little less trapped.

options.text: No adult would understand those chats
options.then: The thought keeps you alone with it, though adults can help.

steps.why: A yes forced by threats isn't a choice, and none of this is your fault.

steps.prompt: That evening, you want someone on your side. Who do you go to?

options.text: Your best friend, who says to call his bluff
options.then: Your friend drafts a reply for you, and your hands shake reading it.

options.text: Varun's friend, to ask him to back off
options.then: Varun hears within the hour and sends a new threat.

options.text: A parent or a teacher you trust
options.then: Your father listens, stays calm, and says you're not in trouble.

options.text: A forum where people share similar stories
options.then: Some stories help, others scare you more, and none know your situation.

steps.why: A trusted adult can protect you in ways a friend or a forum can't.

steps.prompt: Later, you wonder whether to delete all the chats. What do you do?

options.text: Delete everything so there's less to share
options.then: Your side is gone, but he still has his copies.

options.text: Send him a threat of your own
options.then: He screenshots it and says now he has even more to share.

options.text: Keep them, and show them to a trusted adult
options.then: The adult saves copies and says you'll get help together.

options.text: Post about him first, before he can
options.then: Your post spreads fast, and now everyone is asking questions.

steps.why: Keeping the messages helps the people protecting you act on them.

steps.prompt: The next day, you wonder what help exists beyond your family. What comes to mind?

options.text: Help only comes once something worse happens
options.then: The thought makes your fear feel too small to count.

options.text: Reporting it will just get me in trouble
options.then: The worry grows, though you've done nothing wrong.

options.text: Only the police can help, and they'd judge me
options.then: You picture a cold desk, though help can start with one phone call.

options.text: Childline 1098 helps with threats like this
options.then: You save the number, and calling feels possible with an adult beside you.

steps.why: Childline 1098 and a trusted adult can protect you. This is never your fault.

scenarios.debrief: Coercion removes choice. Tell a trusted adult or Childline 1098. It's never your fault.
scenarios.relearn: If a choice is being forced, it isn't a choice; route coercion to a trusted adult.

scenarios.hook: Your partner Simran says protection, if you two ever have sex, is your problem to sort out.

steps.prompt: She says it as if the matter's closed. What do you say?

options.text: Fine, you'll handle all of it
options.then: She looks relieved, and the whole weight lands on you.

options.text: That it's actually her problem, not yours
options.then: She bristles, and now it's a blame game.

options.text: That it's something you'd decide together
options.then: Simran pauses, then admits she'd never seen it as shared.

options.text: That you'll talk about it some other time
options.then: The topic slides away, and so does any plan.

steps.why: Protection is something partners agree on together, not one person's job.

steps.prompt: A few days later, Simran admits she's embarrassed to talk about it. What do you do?

options.text: Drop it to spare her the awkwardness
options.then: Her embarrassment fades, and the question stays unanswered.

options.text: Tell her she needs to grow up about it
options.then: She goes quiet, and talking feels even harder now.

options.text: Ask your friends to explain it to her
options.then: She's mortified that your friends know.

options.text: Say it's awkward for you too, and ask to talk calmly
options.then: She laughs a little, and the topic feels less heavy.

steps.why: Naming the awkwardness together makes an honest talk easier to start.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, the topic comes up again on a walk. What do you two agree?

options.text: That whoever cares more should handle it
options.then: You look at each other, unsure who that is.

options.text: That any plan is one you both agree to first
options.then: Simran nods, and it feels like a real partnership.

options.text: That you'll work it out in the moment
options.then: It sounds easy, but it leaves the plan to chance.

options.text: That she'll handle it after all
options.then: She agrees reluctantly, and it's one person's job again.

steps.why: Agreeing together in a calm moment means neither of you carries it alone.

scenarios.debrief: A real decision here is shared. Both of you weigh in and agree.
scenarios.relearn: A shared decision is made together; one person can't decide protection for both.

scenarios.hook: In your group, dating someone seems to make you cool, and you're tempted to date just for that.

steps.prompt: Karan asks you out, and your friends start cheering. What do you do?

options.text: Say yes for the status, and see how it goes
options.then: Your friends cheer, and you feel oddly far from your own life.

options.text: Say no loudly, to show you don't care
options.then: Karan looks embarrassed, and your friends tease you instead.

options.text: Ask your friends what you should do
options.then: They vote yes, though none of them have to live with it.

options.text: Take a day to think about whether you like him
options.then: Karan says sure, and the cheering fades into the background.

steps.why: Deciding by what you actually feel, not how it looks, keeps the choice yours.

steps.prompt: Later, your friend Zoya says everyone will notice who comes to the farewell with a date. What do you think?

options.text: I'd better make sure I'm seen with someone
options.then: The date starts to matter more than any person.

options.text: Date or no date, it's about what fits me
options.then: The farewell becomes just a party again.

options.text: Maybe I only count if I bring someone
options.then: The doubt grows, though your worth isn't a plus-one.

options.text: I'll go with whoever the group approves of
options.then: The group starts choosing for you, one comment at a time.

steps.why: Your values decide your relationships, not a party or a headcount.

steps.prompt: A week later, a classmate posts a ranking of the coolest couples. What do you do?

options.text: Scroll it twice to see where you'd fit
options.then: Comparing leaves you feeling smaller.

options.text: Comment that rankings are childish
options.then: The thread turns on you, and it drags on for days.

options.text: Ignore it and focus on what matters to you
options.then: You close the app, and the list feels like noise.

options.text: Share it so you can laugh along
options.then: The laughs feel hollow, and someone near the bottom skips lunch.

steps.why: Image isn't a value. Deciding for your real life keeps you off the scoreboard.

scenarios.debrief: Image isn't a value. Decide for your real life, not the audience.
scenarios.relearn: Decide by your values, not by how a choice looks to others.

scenarios.hook: You have questions about sexual health but feel too embarrassed to ask anyone.

steps.prompt: You have Friday afternoon free. What do you do?

options.text: Search online and trust the top result
options.then: The top result is an ad, and the second contradicts it.

options.text: Wait until the questions feel less embarrassing
options.then: Weeks pass, and the embarrassment doesn't shrink on its own.

options.text: Book a visit to an adolescent-friendly clinic
options.then: The booking is simple, and your slot is next Tuesday.

options.text: Ask a friend to ask a doctor for you
options.then: Your friend agrees, then forgets half your questions.

steps.why: Asking a clinician is what maturity looks like, and they hear these questions daily.

steps.prompt: Days later, you picture asking a doctor and worry about being judged. What do you tell yourself?

options.text: Doctors are there to help, not to judge
options.then: The knot in your stomach loosens a little.

options.text: They'll think I'm up to something
options.then: The worry makes the questions feel shameful, though they aren't.

options.text: I'll only ask the less awkward questions
options.then: Your list shrinks to the easy ones, and the important ones stay home.

options.text: I'll pretend it's for a school project
options.then: It might work, but the answers won't be about you.

steps.why: Clinicians are there to inform, not judge. Asking about sexual health is routine care.

steps.prompt: When you do see a doctor, she asks if anything else is on your mind. What do you do?

options.text: Say no, and leave before it gets awkward
options.then: You're outside in two minutes, your biggest question unasked.

options.text: Ask her to email you the answer later
options.then: She says she can't, but she's happy to answer now.

options.text: Ask whether other people ever ask this
options.then: She says yes, often, and waits for you to actually ask it.

options.text: Ask the question you were most nervous about
options.then: She answers it plainly, and you wonder why you worried so long.

steps.why: The question you're most nervous about is often the one most worth asking.

scenarios.debrief: Gather the facts first. Asking isn't a weakness. It's how you decide well.
scenarios.relearn: Asking is what maturity looks like; gather facts before you decide.

scenarios.source: decision skill / pressure to prove love
scenarios.hook: Your boyfriend Rohan keeps saying that if you really loved him, you'd have sex with him.

steps.prompt: He says it again tonight, sounding hurt. What goes through your mind?

options.text: Maybe love does mean saying yes
options.then: The thought sits wrong, and you can't yet say why.

options.text: If I keep saying no, I'll end up losing him
options.then: The fear grows louder than what you actually want.

options.text: Maybe I'm being unfair to him
options.then: Guilt creeps in, though you've done nothing unfair.

options.text: Love isn't proven this way
options.then: You feel clearer, even though his words still sting.

steps.why: 'If you loved me' is pressure, not a reason. Your readiness is yours to decide.

steps.prompt: Rohan texts that he just needs to know you're serious about him. What do you reply?

options.text: That you'll prove it some other way
options.then: He asks how, and the pressure changes shape instead of stopping.

options.text: That you care, and you're not ready yet
options.then: He doesn't reply for an hour, then sends a short okay.

options.text: A long apology for making him doubt you
options.then: He accepts it, and the pressure stays exactly the same.

options.text: That he's a creep for even asking
options.then: He's stung, and the real point gets lost in the fight.

steps.why: Saying both truths plainly keeps your boundary without a fight.

steps.prompt: By the weekend, you feel worn down by it all. Who do you talk to?

options.text: Rohan's sister, hoping she'll talk to him
options.then: She tells Rohan, and he's angry you talked about him.

options.text: A friend who says everyone gives in eventually
options.then: Her words make your no feel temporary.

options.text: Ms. D'Souza, the school counsellor you trust
options.then: She listens and says love never needs that kind of proof.

options.text: An advice forum online
options.then: The replies are a mix of jokes and lectures.

steps.why: A trusted adult can help you hold your ground. The pressure is not your fault.

steps.prompt: Rohan says he'll stop asking, but he goes cold whenever you meet. What do you take from it?

options.text: I should make it up to him somehow
options.then: You start planning how to fix his mood, and your own feelings slip away.

options.text: At least he stopped asking, so it's fine
options.then: The silent pressure keeps working on you all the same.

options.text: Going cold is pressure too, and I can see it
options.then: Seeing it clearly, you stop trying to earn his warmth back.

options.text: I'll go cold on him too
options.then: The two of you go quiet, and nothing gets said.

steps.why: Pressure can be quiet too. Noticing it keeps the choice yours, and it's never your fault.

scenarios.debrief: Love isn't a test you pass by giving in. Your readiness decides, and pressure is never your fault.
scenarios.relearn: 'If you loved me' is pressure, not a reason; your readiness decides.

scenarios.source: decision skill / one fact changes it
scenarios.hook: You'd half-decided the pill was enough, then a clinic leaflet said it doesn't cover STIs.

steps.prompt: You'd already told a friend your plan. What do you do?

options.text: Stick with it, since you've told people
options.then: Your plan stays tidy, with a gap you now know about.

options.text: Decide the leaflet must be out of date
options.then: You set it aside, and the doubt follows you home.

options.text: Update your plan to fit the new fact
options.then: It takes a moment, but the plan feels more solid.

options.text: Drop the whole plan out of confusion
options.then: You're back at the start with fewer answers.

steps.why: Updating on a verified fact is part of deciding well, not a failure of nerve.

steps.prompt: Your friend Pallavi hears about the leaflet and says changing plans makes people look flaky. What do you think?

options.text: She's right. Sticking to a plan matters most
options.then: Looking consistent starts to matter more than the gap.

options.text: Changing on a real fact is sensible
options.then: Pallavi shrugs, and you notice you don't need her to agree.

options.text: I'll keep any change to myself
options.then: You keep two stories straight, and it's tiring.

options.text: Maybe I'm silly for not knowing sooner
options.then: You start feeling small for learning something new.

steps.why: Consistency isn't the goal. A choice that fits the facts is.

steps.prompt: A month later, a stranger online posts a scary new claim. What do you do?

options.text: Change your plan right away, just in case
options.then: Your plan shifts again, on nothing solid.

options.text: Ignore all new information from now on

steps.prompt: Siddharth says: "You'll miss out on so much, though."

options.text: "I'm not missing anything, trust me."

options.text: "Maybe. I'm okay with that trade."
options.then: He shrugs. "I guess everyone's different."

options.text: "Easy for you to say. You're dating."
options.then: "That's not the point," he says, annoyed.

steps.why: Admitting the trade-off calmly shows you weighed it, which makes the choice solid.

steps.prompt: Siddharth asks: "Whatever you decide, what if you regret it later?"

options.text: "Then it's your fault for not stopping me."

options.text: "I won't. I'm never wrong about these things."
options.then: He laughs. "Okay, sure."

options.text: "Then I'd better just do what everyone does."
options.then: He shrugs, and your careful reasons slip away.

options.text: "Then I'll own it and adjust. It's my call."
options.then: He nods. "Honestly, that's pretty solid."

scenarios.hook: You and Meher are kissing, and you want to be sure it's a real yes before anything more.
scenarios.setup: She pulls back a little and smiles at you.

steps.prompt: Meher asks: "What's wrong? You've gone quiet."

options.text: "Nothing. Let's keep going."
options.then: She hesitates, and you can't tell what she's thinking.

options.text: "You're okay with this, right? Of course you are."
options.then: She laughs a little, unsure. "Um, I guess?"

options.text: "I was thinking about earlier, when you said yes."
options.then: "Earlier was earlier," she says softly.

options.text: "Nothing's wrong. Do you actually want this too?"
options.then: She thinks. "I like kissing you. I'm not sure about more."

steps.why: Asking openly whether she wants this is the only way to know it's a real yes.

steps.prompt: Meher says: "I'm not sure I want to go any further."

options.text: "Then we stop here. Not sure means not now."
options.then: She relaxes. "Thanks. I really like that you asked."

options.text: "Okay, but you seemed into it a minute ago."
options.then: Her smile fades. "I was. I'm telling you now."

options.text: "Come on, just a little more?"
options.then: She pulls away. "I said I'm not sure."

options.text: "Is it something I did wrong?"
options.then: "No," she says. "It's just how I feel."

steps.why: Only a clear, free yes counts. Unsure means stop, without argument.

steps.prompt: Meher asks: "Are you upset with me?"

options.text: "A little, but I'll get over it."
options.then: She looks guilty, and the moment gets heavy.

options.text: "No. Just tell me when you're ready."
options.then: She nods, but it sounds a bit like a deadline.

options.text: "Not at all. I'm glad you told me."
options.then: She smiles and squeezes your hand.

options.text: "Should I be? You did start it."
options.then: Her face falls. "I didn't mean to lead you on."

steps.why: Being glad she spoke up makes it safe for both of you to say what you feel.

scenarios.relearn: Checking your partner genuinely wants this is part of a sound decision.

scenarios.hook: Your aunt Pushpa has brought a boy's biodata and wants to fix a meeting with his family.

steps.prompt: Aunt Pushpa says: "He's a good boy. Let's meet his family on Sunday."

options.text: "I have exams. Maybe after that."
options.then: "After exams, then," she says, writing it down. "Not a day later."

options.text: "I'll decide about marriage in my own time."
options.then: She blinks. "Your own time? At your age?"

options.text: "Why are you always interfering?"
options.then: Her face hardens. "I'm trying to help this family."

options.text: "Ask Mummy. Whatever she says."
options.then: "Your mother will agree," she says, reaching for her phone.

steps.why: Saying plainly that the timing is yours is clearer than an excuse.

steps.prompt: Aunt Pushpa says: "Girls who wait too long don't get good proposals."

options.text: "Maybe you're right. I hadn't thought of that."
options.then: She nods, satisfied. "Good. Now you're thinking."

options.text: "Good proposals? Like I'm a product?"
options.then: "Don't twist my words," she snaps.

options.text: "That isn't true, and the timing is mine."
options.then: She sighs. "You young people and your timelines."

options.text: "Let's not talk about this now."
options.then: "Then when?" she asks. "Sunday is coming."

steps.why: Calmly naming a myth as a myth keeps your timeline yours without a fight.

steps.prompt: As she gathers the papers, Aunt Pushpa asks: "So tell me, what do you want?"

options.text: "I don't know. Whatever's best, I suppose."
options.then: "Then leave it to us," she says, relieved.

options.text: "Just to be left alone by this family."
options.then: She looks hurt. "We only want good things for you."

options.text: "Nothing. I just don't like this boy."
options.then: "Then we'll find another," she says brightly.

options.text: "To finish my studies, then decide myself."
options.then: She's quiet a moment. "Your studies matter that much?"

steps.why: Saying what you do want gives her something real to respect.

steps.prompt: Aunt Pushpa says: "I'll talk to your parents and let them settle it."

options.text: "Then I'll get my cousins to back me up."

options.text: "I'll talk to them, and ask my teacher to help."
options.then: She raises an eyebrow. "A teacher? Fine. Talk to them."

options.text: "They'd never. They love me more than you."
options.then: Her eyes narrow. "That's a hurtful thing to say."

options.text: "Then there's no point. They'll decide anyway."
options.then: She nods. "Sensible. I'll tell them you agree."

steps.why: A trusted adult can back you up, so you don't hold the line alone. The pressure isn't your fault.

scenarios.relearn: You can hold your own timeline respectfully when family pushes.

options.text: "The clinic. It's my health, not a bargain."
options.then: "Fair," he says. "Tell me if the clinic's any good."

options.text: "Not yours. You always mess things up."

options.text: "It's probably nothing. Just a weird guy."
options.then: She sits beside you. "Even if it feels small, I'm listening."

options.text: "I think I might have led him on."
options.then: She shakes her head. "Whatever happened, it's not on you."

options.text: "Thank you. What can we do next?"

options.text: "I'll confront him myself tomorrow."

options.text: "Can you stop him without telling anyone?"
options.then: "I'll help, but a few people may need to know to keep you safe."

options.text: "Won't they get me into trouble?"

options.text: "Only if they promise it stays secret forever."

steps.prompt: Afterwards, Aunt Farah asks: "How are you feeling now?"

options.text: "Like I should have handled it on my own."

options.text: "Like it's over, so I don't need more help."
options.then: "Maybe," she says gently, "but I'll keep checking on you."

options.text: "Like I should warn everyone at tuition myself."

options.text: "Scared, but lighter now that you know."
