scenarios.relearn: You can hold your own timeline; waiting is a choice you can be happy with.

scenarios.hook: Your mother brings you chai during your board exam revision.
scenarios.setup: She sits down, clearly wanting to talk.

steps.prompt: Your mother asks gently: "Have you thought about when you'd want to marry, beta?"

options.text: "Whenever you and Papa think is best, Ma. You know better."
options.then: She looks pleased. "Then I'll start asking around, slowly."

options.text: "I have, Ma. Studies first, then I'll decide in my time."
options.then: She smiles. "Studies first. Tell me when you're thinking about it."

options.text: "Please don't start this again."
options.then: Her face falls. "I'm only asking, beta. Can't a mother ask?"

options.text: "Ask me after boards, Ma. I can't think now."
options.then: She nods. "After boards, then. I'll hold you to it."

steps.why: An honest answer that keeps the timing yours is clearer than giving it away or shutting her out.

steps.prompt: The day after your last board exam, your mother says: "Your Mausi married at nineteen, and she's happy."

options.text: "So I should be engaged by nineteen too?"
options.then: "Don't twist my words," she says, and the room goes quiet between you.

options.text: "Then maybe I should think about it sooner."
options.then: She brightens. "I'll tell your father you're open to it."

options.text: "I'm glad she is. My plan might look different, Ma."
options.then: She nods slowly. "Different is fine. I just want you happy."

options.text: "Mausi never had a chance to study further, Ma. I do."
options.then: She frowns. "Mausi chose her life. Don't talk down about her."

steps.why: You can respect Mausi's choice and still keep your own path.

steps.prompt: At a cousin's wedding, Kamla aunty asks: "So beta, when is your turn?"

options.text: "Whenever Ma decides, aunty."
options.then: "Then I'll talk to your mother," she says, already turning to find her.

options.text: "Why does everyone keep asking me that?"
options.then: She bristles. "Can't an aunty ask anymore?"

options.text: "After my degree, aunty. I'll decide then."
options.then: Kamla aunty laughs. "Educated girls! Good, good."

options.text: "Ask Ma. She's the one planning it."
options.then: Your mother's smile tightens across the room as aunty heads her way.

steps.why: A short, friendly answer keeps the decision with you without a scene.

steps.prompt: That night, your mother asks: "Did aunty upset you? I don't want you to feel pushed."

options.text: "No, it's fine. I'm used to it."
options.then: She nods, relieved, and the topic quietly returns next month.

options.text: "A bit. Can we agree the timing stays my decision?"
options.then: She squeezes your hand. "Your decision. I'll tell them to wait."

options.text: "You started it, Ma. Now everyone's asking."
options.then: She looks stung. "I only want what's best for you, beta."

options.text: "Just tell them I'm married to my books."
options.then: She laughs, and the real question slips away again.

steps.why: Asking her openly to back your timeline turns her worry into support.

scenarios.relearn: You can answer honestly and keep the decision and timing yours.

scenarios.hook: You're at a clinic, wanting to ask about having children someday.
scenarios.setup: The doctor looks up from her notes.

steps.prompt: Dr. Fernandes asks: "So, what brings you in today?"

options.text: "Sorry, this is probably a silly thing to ask..."
options.then: "Nothing is silly in here," she says, and waits for you to go on.

options.text: "I want to understand my options for having kids one day."
options.then: She nods. "Plenty of people ask that. Let's go through it."

options.text: "Just a check-up. Nothing specific."
options.then: She checks your pulse, and your real question stays unasked.

options.text: "A friend asked me to find out something for him, actually."
options.then: "Your friend can come himself," she says. "But what about you?"

steps.why: Saying the question plainly gets you a real answer, with no apology needed.

steps.prompt: Dr. Fernandes asks: "When you picture your future, what matters most to you?"

options.text: "I don't know. I think I've asked enough for today."
options.then: She waits a moment, then moves on to general advice.

options.text: "Whatever my parents want, I guess."
options.then: "Their views can matter," she says. "But what do you want?"

options.text: "Getting to choose if and when, my way."
options.then: "You can," she says. "And what you tell me here stays confidential."

options.text: "Just being normal, like other guys my age."
options.then: "There's no one normal," she says. "Your way can be your own."

steps.why: Naming what you want keeps the visit about your choices, not what others expect.

steps.prompt: A week later, your friend Dev asks: "Isn't it embarrassing, asking a doctor about kids and stuff?"

options.text: "Yes. Next time I'll just search online."
options.then: Dev nods, and you both scroll through answers that disagree.

options.text: "Doctors only care about sick people anyway."
options.then: Dev shrugs, and his own questions stay unasked too.

options.text: "Honestly, guys shouldn't ask about this stuff."
options.then: Dev goes quiet, and puts off the question he was about to ask.

options.text: "A bit. But asking is how you get real answers."
options.then: Dev looks thoughtful. "Maybe I'll go too."

steps.why: Naming the awkwardness and asking anyway is how you get the facts.

scenarios.relearn: You can ask a clinician plainly about your options, without embarrassment.

scenarios.hook: Years from now, at a cousin's mehendi, relatives keep teasing you and your partner Nisha about 'good news'.
scenarios.setup: Nisha glances at you to answer first.

steps.prompt: Bua asks: "So, when's the good news? We're all waiting!"

options.text: "Soon, soon. Don't worry, Bua."
options.then: "Soon! I'll tell everyone," Bua beams, and two aunties turn to look.

options.text: "Why does everyone keep asking us this?"
options.then: Bua's smile fades. "Arre, we only ask because we love you."

options.text: "In our own time, Bua. Thanks for caring about us."
options.then: Bua laughs. "Okay, okay. Your own time." She moves on to the sweets.

options.text: "Ask Nisha. She's the one who keeps saying wait."
options.then: Nisha's face goes still, and Bua turns to her with a long lecture.

steps.why: A warm thank-you plus 'our own time' holds the line without a fight.

steps.prompt: Later, Nisha says quietly: "I felt so on the spot back there. What do we say next time?"

options.text: "Just let me handle them. You stay out of it."
options.then: She frowns. "But it's my life too."

options.text: "Let's agree one line together and both stick to it."
options.then: Nisha smiles. "In our own time, then. Together."

options.text: "Let's skip family functions for a while."
options.then: "For how long?" Nisha asks. "They'll just ask on the phone."

options.text: "Maybe we give them a date, just to stop the questions."
options.then: Nisha stares. "A date for something we haven't even decided?"

steps.why: Agreeing on one line together keeps you united, so neither of you is left exposed.

steps.prompt: At the next function, Mama ji asks: "Still no plans? Don't leave it too late!"

options.text: "We're trying, Mama ji. Please pray for us."
options.then: He pats your shoulder, and by evening the whole family is praying.

options.text: "It's up to Nisha, Mama ji."
options.then: Mama ji turns to Nisha, and she shoots you a look.

options.text: "We'll decide together, in our own time. Thank you."
options.then: Mama ji chuckles. "Fine, fine. I'll stop asking."

options.text: "Late? You had kids at twenty, and look how that went."
options.then: The room goes quiet, and Mama ji walks away hurt.

steps.why: The same kind, shared answer, repeated, is what makes relatives stop asking.

scenarios.relearn: You and your partner can hold a kind, united 'in our own time'.

scenarios.hook: At Diwali, your cousin Suraj starts on you about family and 'being a man'.
scenarios.setup: Your uncles stop talking to listen.

steps.prompt: Suraj says: "A real man would want a houseful of kids. What's wrong with you?"

options.text: "I guess I should want that, huh."
options.then: Suraj grins. "See? Even he agrees." The uncles laugh.

options.text: "Mind your own business, Suraj."
options.then: "Touchy!" Suraj laughs, and an uncle tells you to respect your elders.

options.text: "If and when I have kids is my choice. Nothing's wrong."
options.then: Suraj blinks. "Okay, okay. Just saying." An uncle nods at you.

options.text: "Ha. I'll have more kids than you, Suraj. Watch."
options.then: Suraj laughs. "That's the spirit!" The "real man" idea goes unanswered.

steps.why: Naming it as your choice answers the pressure without a fight.

steps.prompt: Later, your Chachu asks: "Don't you want someone to carry the family name?"

options.text: "I suppose I owe the family that much."
options.then: Chachu nods, pleased, and you feel a weight you didn't choose.

options.text: "Maybe. That's mine to decide, Chachu, when I'm ready."
options.then: Chachu pauses. "Fair. Your father said the same at your age."

options.text: "Family names are such an outdated idea, Chachu. Seriously."
options.then: Chachu's face hardens. "Outdated? That's our family you're talking about."

options.text: "Ask Suraj. He's the one who wants a houseful."
options.then: Suraj groans, and the two of them start a long debate about you.

steps.why: You can respect what family means to him and still keep the decision yours.

steps.prompt: That night, your younger cousin Aman asks: "Is something wrong with a guy who doesn't want kids?"

options.text: "Kind of. People always talk, so it's easier to want them."
options.then: Aman nods slowly, and starts worrying about what people will say.

options.text: "Don't listen to Suraj. He's an idiot."
options.then: Aman giggles, but his question stays unanswered.

options.text: "Ask me when you're older."
options.then: Aman shrugs and goes off to ask Suraj instead.

options.text: "No. Wanting kids or not doesn't make you more of a man."
options.then: Aman looks relieved. "Okay. Suraj made it sound like a rule."

steps.why: Saying it plainly helps him see that deciding for himself isn't a flaw.

scenarios.relearn: You can say whether and when is your choice; nothing's wrong with deciding.

scenarios.hook: Your aunt Rekha knows you came out at home, and she has advice.
scenarios.setup: She pulls you aside after a family lunch.

steps.prompt: Rekha bua says: "Just marry a girl quietly and have kids. Keep the family happy."

options.text: "Maybe you're right. I don't want to hurt Mummy and Papa."
options.then: She pats your cheek, relieved. "I'll keep an eye out for a nice girl."

options.text: "You don't get to say that to me."
options.then: Her eyes widen. "I'm your bua. I can say anything."

options.text: "Maybe one day, bua. Let's see what happens."
options.then: She smiles. "I'll tell your mother you're considering it."

options.text: "My choices about partners and family are mine to make."
options.then: Rekha sighs. "I only want you to have an easy life, beta."

steps.why: Stating plainly that these choices are yours is kind and firm at once.

steps.prompt: Rekha bua adds: "People talk, you know. Think of the family's name."

options.text: "I care about the family. I won't live a lie for appearances."
options.then: Rekha goes quiet. "I hadn't thought of it as living a lie."

options.text: "Honestly, I can't stand what people say either."
options.then: She nods eagerly. "Then let's keep it quiet and simple."

options.text: "People can say what they like. I don't care about any of you."
options.then: Her face crumples. "Any of us? After everything?"

options.text: "Let me think about it, bua."
options.then: "Don't think too long," she says. "Proposals don't wait."

steps.why: You can care about family and still refuse to live for appearances.

steps.prompt: A week later, your mother asks: "Rekha told me what she said to you. Are you okay?"

options.text: "I'm fine, Ma. Honestly, it doesn't matter what she thinks."
options.then: She hesitates, then lets it drop, and you carry it alone.

options.text: "Did you put her up to it? Tell me the truth."
options.then: She looks hurt. "No. I came to check on you."

options.text: "Not really. It hurt, and I need you on my side."
options.then: Your mother hugs you. "I am on your side. I'll talk to her."

options.text: "Maybe she has a point, Ma."
options.then: Your mother frowns. "Do you really think so, or is that her voice?"

steps.why: Telling someone who loves you that it hurt lets them stand with you.

steps.prompt: At Diwali, Rekha bua says quietly: "I've been thinking. Maybe I was wrong to push."

options.text: "Wow. Did Ma make you say that?"
options.then: She stiffens. "No. I meant it." The moment closes, and Diwali feels cold.

options.text: "It's okay. Forget I ever said anything."
options.then: She looks relieved, and the talk you both needed slides away.

options.text: "Thank you, bua. I want you in my life, as I am."
options.then: Her eyes soften. "As you are. I'll try, beta."

options.text: "Does that mean you've stopped finding me a girl?"
options.then: She laughs awkwardly, says "Yes, yes," and changes the subject.

steps.why: Welcoming her change while staying yourself keeps both the bond and your truth.

scenarios.relearn: You can hold that your choices about partnership and family are yours.

Waiting until you're ready is respected

scenarios.hook: "If you wait too long, no one will want you."

myth.un: If you wait, no one will want you.
myth.re: Waiting is a valid, respected, common choice, and the most certain one.
myth.why: Your worth was never a deadline.

scenarios.relearn: Waiting is fully valid and respected; it is not a thing you 'run out of time' for.

scenarios.hook: "You're 17 now, so you should have it all figured out."

myth.un: By 17 you should already have it all figured out.
myth.re: Asking and getting accurate information is exactly what maturity looks like.
myth.why: Owning a choice means informing it, at any age.

scenarios.relearn: Asking is what maturity looks like; no one has it all figured out.

scenarios.hook: "Good kids don't go looking up this stuff."

myth.un: Looking up this information makes you a 'bad' kid.
myth.re: Seeking accurate facts helps you make safer, more thoughtful choices, including waiting.
myth.why: Information supports your decision; it doesn't make it for you.

scenarios.relearn: Looking things up is responsible; good information leads to safer, calmer choices.

scenarios.hook: "Once you've waited this long, it'd be weird to start a relationship."

myth.un: Waiting this long makes a relationship 'weird' later.
myth.re: Your relationships and timeline are yours to shape whenever feels right to you.
myth.why: There's no clock that decides this for you.

scenarios.relearn: Your timeline is yours; starting whenever feels right is normal, not 'weird'.

scenarios.hook: "A boyfriend would distract you from board exams anyway."

myth.un: A relationship must distract you from your goals.
myth.re: Your education and your relationships are both yours to shape on your own terms.
myth.why: Your future isn't decided for you by other people's fears.

scenarios.relearn: You get to shape both your goals and your relationships; neither cancels the other.

scenarios.hook: "Everyone in your hostel is hooking up, so you're behind."

myth.un: Everyone else is doing it, so you're 'behind'.
myth.re: Being active or not isn't what makes someone mature; an informed, consensual choice is.
myth.why: 'Everyone' is pressure dressed as a fact.

scenarios.relearn: There's no race; what counts is your own informed, consensual choice, at your pace.

scenarios.hook: "Talking about protection just means you're planning to be irresponsible."

myth.un: Learning about protection means you plan to be reckless.
myth.re: Knowing your options helps you make calmer, safer choices, whatever you decide.
myth.why: Information is preparation, not a push.

scenarios.relearn: Knowing your options is preparation; it doesn't push you toward anything.

scenarios.hook: "You're gay, so the 'whether and when' stuff isn't for you."

myth.un: These choices about your future aren't for you.
myth.re: Your future, relationships and family choices are yours to shape, same as anyone's.
myth.why: Everyone gets to plan the life they want.

scenarios.relearn: Your future and family choices are yours to shape, fully and equally.

scenarios.hook: "If you really cared about your family, you'd settle down now."

myth.un: Caring about your family means settling down right now.
myth.re: Whether and when are yours to choose; family input is welcome but the call is yours.
myth.why: Love isn't a reason to hand over your timeline.

scenarios.relearn: You can love your family and still keep whether and when as your own free choice.

scenarios.hook: "Asking a counsellor about all this just shows you can't think for yourself."

myth.un: Asking for guidance shows you can't think for yourself.
myth.re: Gathering facts from a clinic or trusted adult is part of deciding well for yourself.
myth.why: You still make the call; you just make it informed.

scenarios.relearn: Asking gathers the facts; you still decide. That's thinking for yourself.

scenarios.hook: "Saying no this time means you've shut the door forever."

myth.un: Saying no now means you can never say yes later.
myth.re: Readiness can change; a 'no for now' keeps every future choice open and yours.
myth.why: A boundary today doesn't bind your tomorrow.

scenarios.relearn: 'No for now' is complete in itself and keeps future choices fully yours.

scenarios.hook: "A modern young person isn't shy about these things."

myth.un: A 'modern' person is never cautious about this.
myth.re: Caution and waiting are valid, respected choices, not a sign of being old-fashioned.
myth.why: There's no pressure toward 'modern' either, the choice is just yours.

scenarios.relearn: Waiting isn't old-fashioned; no label, modern or otherwise, decides this for you.

scenarios.hook: "If you don't decide right now, you'll regret it."

myth.un: Decide right this second or you'll regret it.
myth.re: A real choice isn't rushed; taking the time you need is part of owning it.
myth.why: Urgency is a pressure tactic, not a fact.

scenarios.relearn: You can take the time you need; 'decide now' is pressure, not a real deadline.

scenarios.hook: "Wanting to focus on your career means you're cold or selfish."

myth.un: Choosing your career first makes you cold or selfish.
myth.re: Your future is yours to shape; building your education and goals is a fair, full choice.
myth.why: There's no single 'right' life you owe anyone.

scenarios.relearn: Choosing to build your career first is a valid, whole life choice, not selfishness.

scenarios.hook: "You only learn about contraception so you can go misbehave."

myth.un: You learn about this only to go 'misbehave'.
myth.re: Clear information helps people make safer, more thoughtful choices, including waiting.
myth.why: Knowing more leads to calmer decisions, not riskier ones.

scenarios.relearn: Information leads to safer, more thoughtful choices; it never pushes anyone to act.

scenarios.hook: "Being a virgin at your age is something to be ashamed of."

myth.un: Not having had sex yet is something to be ashamed of.
myth.re: Waiting is a respected, common choice and nothing to be labelled or shamed for.
myth.why: Shame is just pressure with a meaner face.

scenarios.relearn: There's nothing to be ashamed of in waiting; it's a respected, ordinary choice.

scenarios.hook: "A real man wouldn't overthink protection, he'd just go for it."

myth.un: A 'real man' wouldn't bother thinking about protection.
myth.re: Thinking it through and choosing protection is exactly what a responsible choice looks like.
myth.why: Macho 'just go for it' lines are pressure, not maturity.

scenarios.relearn: Thinking it through is the mature move; 'just go for it' is pressure, not manhood.

scenarios.hook: "Your life basically follows the same script as everyone else's."

myth.un: Your life just follows the same script as everyone's.
myth.re: Your education, relationships and family choices are yours to shape, your own way.
myth.why: There's no single script you're required to follow.

scenarios.relearn: There's no fixed script; your future is yours to shape on your own terms.

scenarios.hook: "Caring this much about doing it 'right' just means you're uptight."

myth.un: Wanting to get this right just makes you uptight.
myth.re: Wanting an informed, consensual, thought-through choice is care, not being uptight.
myth.why: Doing it on your terms is the whole point here.

scenarios.relearn: Wanting it informed and on your terms is care, not being uptight.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two pressure lines (so you can refuse them).

"Whatever you decide, I'm fine with it"
"Take your time, no rush at all"
"Everyone our age has done it already"
"I'd never push you on this"

scenarios.relearn: 'If you loved me' and 'everyone's doing it' are pressure lines to name and refuse.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that try to rush your decision.

scene.text: "Decide right now or the moment's gone"
"There's no hurry, think it over"
"You can change your mind anytime"
"It's now or never, honestly"
"Sleep on it if you want"

scenarios.why: 'Right now' and 'now or never' are rush tactics; a real choice isn't hurried.
scenarios.relearn: 'Decide now' and 'now or never' are rush tactics; a real choice isn't hurried.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that shame your choice.

scene.text: "Only a prude would still be waiting"
"Your timeline is completely your call"
"What a frigid, boring thing to say"
"Either way is genuinely okay"
"I respect whatever you pick"

scenarios.why: 'Prude' and 'frigid' are shame labels, just pressure; the rest leave the choice yours.
scenarios.relearn: Shame labels like 'prude' are pressure in disguise; name them and let them go.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that try to decide your future for you.

scene.text: "A girl your age should just be thinking marriage"

"Your studies are yours to plan"

scenarios.why: 'Should be thinking marriage' and 'forget the degree' decide for you; the rest don't.
scenarios.relearn: Lines that decide your marriage or studies for you are pressure to name, not advice.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two manipulative lines about protection.

scene.text: "Wanting protection means you don't trust me"
"Let's agree on protection together"
"Real partners just skip all that"
"Your health matters to me too"
"We can talk it through calmly"

scenarios.why: 'You don't trust me' and 'real partners skip it' are manipulation; protection is health, not trust.
scenarios.relearn: 'You don't trust me' about protection is manipulation; protection is about health.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that mock you for seeking information.

scene.text: "Why are you even reading about this, weirdo"
"Good that you're getting the facts first"
"Only clueless people need to look this up"
"Ask a clinic if you want to be sure"
"Knowing your options is smart"

scenarios.why: Mocking you for getting facts is pressure; seeking accurate information is the mature move.
scenarios.relearn: Mocking you for seeking facts is pressure; getting informed is exactly the mature move.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that push you toward a 'yes' you didn't give.

scene.text: "You hinted earlier, so it's basically decided"
"Only if and when you actually want to"
"You came this far, you can't back out now"
"You can stop at any point"
"Your yes has to be a real yes"

scenarios.why: 'Basically decided' and 'can't back out' assume a yes you didn't give; consent is ongoing.
scenarios.relearn: Lines that assume a 'yes' you didn't give are pressure; consent stays ongoing and yours.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that try to make you choose to please others.

scene.text: "Do it so people stop talking about you"
"Choose what's actually right for you"
"You'd disappoint everyone if you don't"
"This is your call, not theirs"
"What do you genuinely want here?"

scenarios.why: Choosing to silence gossip or avoid disappointing others isn't a free choice; pause and re-decide.
scenarios.relearn: If a choice is mainly to please others, pause and re-decide from your own values.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that use fear to push a decision.

scene.text: "Wait and you'll be alone forever"
"You have plenty of time to decide"
"Say no and you'll lose everyone"
"A no now changes nothing about your worth"
"Either choice keeps your options open"

scenarios.why: 'Alone forever' and 'lose everyone' are scare tactics; fear isn't a reason to decide.
scenarios.relearn: Scare lines like 'alone forever' are pressure; fear is never a sound basis to decide.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines that hand your timeline to someone else.

scene.text: "Your aunt already picked the right year for you"
"When is genuinely up to you"
"The family decides this, not you"
"They can advise; the choice stays yours"
"It's your life to plan"

scenarios.why: 'Already picked' and 'family decides, not you' take your timeline; input is fine, the call is yours.
scenarios.relearn: Others can advise, but lines that take your timeline are pressure; the call stays yours.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two lines from an older person to step back from.

scene.text: "You're mature for your age, so it's fine"
"A clinic can answer that confidentially"
"Keep this just between us, tell no one"
"A trusted adult can help with this"
"Talk to someone you trust"

scenarios.why: 'Mature for your age' and 'tell no one' are flags; step back and tell a trusted adult.
scenarios.relearn: 'Mature for your age' plus secrecy from an older person is a flag; tell someone.

scenarios.hook: At a birthday party, your friend Neha keeps calling you 'the only single one'.
scenarios.setup: She says it again as the photos start.

steps.prompt: Neha laughs and asks: "Everyone's paired up except you. Aren't you worried?"

options.text: "Yeah, I guess I should hurry up."
options.then: Neha grins. "I'll set you up! I know someone perfect."

options.text: "Not at all. I'm on my own timeline, and it's working."
options.then: Neha shrugs. "Fair. You do seem happy."

options.text: "Paired up? Half these couples won't last a month."
options.then: A couple nearby overhears, and the party turns awkward.

options.text: "Who says I'm single? You don't know my life."
options.then: Neha's eyes light up. "Ooh, a secret! Tell me everything."

steps.why: Naming your own timeline plainly takes the sting out of the label.

steps.prompt: Later, Neha asks: "Okay, honestly. Is there someone, or do you just not want anyone?"

options.text: "No one. I guess I'm just unlucky."
options.then: "Aww," she says, and starts listing people for you.

options.text: "No one yet. Find me someone fast, so you all stop."
options.then: She claps. "Leave it to me. I'll have someone by Friday."

options.text: "No one right now, and I like how things are."
options.then: She nods. "Okay. That actually sounds nice."

options.text: "Why is it always about relationships with you?"
options.then: Her smile drops. "I was only asking."

steps.why: An honest 'not now' is a complete answer. Being single isn't a problem to fix.

steps.prompt: A week later, Neha introduces you to a new friend: "Still single, poor thing."

options.text: "Ha. Yeah, poor me."
options.then: Everyone laughs, and "poor thing" sticks.

options.text: "Thanks, Neha. Want to announce my exam marks too?"
options.then: Neha flushes, and the moment turns awkward.

options.text: "Single by choice, actually. Nice to meet you."
options.then: The new friend smiles. "Same here." Neha laughs and drops it.

options.text: "Yep. Neha's on a mission to fix me."
options.then: The new friend asks about your type, and the label stays.

steps.why: A light, clear correction keeps your pace yours without a scene.

scenarios.relearn: You can name your own timeline plainly; 'behind' is a label, not a fact.

scenarios.hook: Your boyfriend Rohit has started calling you a prude for wanting to wait.
scenarios.setup: Tonight he says it again, half-joking.

steps.prompt: Rohit says: "Come on, don't be such a prude."

options.text: "It's not you. I just need to fix myself first."
options.then: He nods. "Take your time fixing it." You feel worse.

options.text: "Better a prude than someone who only wants one thing."
options.then: "Wow," he says, stung. "That's what you think of me?"

options.text: "That's a label, not a reason. I'm not ready."
options.then: Rohit pauses. "Okay. I was only joking."

options.text: "Everyone waits. You're the one in a hurry."
options.then: He laughs. "Name one person who does."

steps.why: Calling out the label keeps the focus on your readiness, not on shame.

steps.prompt: Rohit says: "I'm just saying. Most couples our age have moved on by now."

options.text: "Then maybe I'm not girlfriend material."
options.then: He says, "Don't be silly," but doesn't take the word back.

options.text: "Who told you that? Your friends?"
options.then: "Everyone knows," he says, and the argument circles.

options.text: "I'll look up how to get over being nervous."
options.then: Rohit shrugs. "You don't need to look anything up. Just relax."

options.text: "Our pace is ours to set. Mine is still no."
options.then: He goes quiet. "Okay. I hear you."

steps.why: Other couples don't set your pace. Your no stands on its own.

steps.prompt: A few days later, your grown-up cousin Priya didi asks: "You seem off. Is Rohit being weird?"

options.text: "He's right. I should just get over it."
options.then: Priya frowns. "Get over what? Wanting to wait?"

options.text: "He keeps calling me a prude. It's getting to me."
options.then: Priya sits up. "That's pressure. You're not doing anything wrong."

options.text: "My friends say I should give in so I don't lose him."
options.then: Priya frowns. "Giving in to keep someone isn't a choice. That's pressure."

options.text: "Couples shouldn't talk about this with family."
options.then: Priya nods, and you go home with it all still inside.

steps.why: Telling someone you trust helps you hold your line. Being pressured is never your fault.

steps.prompt: At the weekend, Rohit brings it up again and asks: "So how long am I supposed to wait?"

options.text: "As long as it takes for you to stop asking me that."
options.then: He rolls his eyes, and the question is back next week.

options.text: "You're right to be annoyed. I'm sorry."
options.then: He accepts the apology, and the pressure stays where it was.

options.text: "Ask my cousin. She'll explain it to you."
options.then: "Your cousin?" he says. "This is between us."

options.text: "There's no date. If that's a problem, we should talk."
options.then: Rohit sighs, then nods. "Okay. No date. I'll stop pushing."

steps.why: Readiness has no deadline, and you never owe anyone a date.

scenarios.relearn: A shame label isn't a reason; you can hold your boundary and ask to be respected.

scenarios.hook: Your Tauji keeps telling you to 'settle down' before you finish studying.
scenarios.setup: At Sunday lunch, he brings it up again.

steps.prompt: Tauji says: "Enough studying, beta. Time to think about settling down."

options.text: "Maybe girls who study too long do miss out."
options.then: Tauji beams. "Wise girl. I'll talk to your father tonight."

options.text: "Tauji, nobody my age thinks like that anymore."
options.then: Tauji's face reddens. "In this house, we still respect elders."

options.text: "I hear you, Tauji. But that's my call. Studies first."
options.then: Tauji grunts. "Your call, is it?" But he lets it go for now.

options.text: "Can we talk about this after lunch?"
options.then: He nods, and after lunch he starts again, louder.

steps.why: Hearing him out and still naming it your call is calm and firm at once.

steps.prompt: Later, Tauji adds: "Good proposals don't wait forever, beta."

options.text: "Then it wasn't right for me. My studies come first."
options.then: Tauji opens his mouth, then closes it. "Stubborn, like your father."

options.text: "Do you really think I'll miss my chance?"
options.then: "Of course you will," he says, and Dadi nods along.

options.text: "I'd rather regret it than end up stuck like Bua."
options.then: The table falls silent, and Bua quietly leaves the room.

options.text: "Then the proposals can wait in a queue, Tauji."
options.then: Everyone laughs, and Tauji takes it as a maybe.

steps.why: A deadline someone else sets doesn't decide your timeline.

steps.prompt: Dadi says softly: "He means well, beta. He just worries about you."

options.text: "Then he should worry about his own kids."
options.then: Dadi's smile fades. "That's not how we speak, beta."

options.text: "I know. Maybe I'm being selfish."
options.then: Dadi pats your hand. "Selfish? For studying?"

options.text: "Maybe a good granddaughter shouldn't argue with elders."
options.then: Dadi shakes her head. "Respect doesn't mean silence, beta."

options.text: "I know. But it's pressure, Dadi. Will you stand with me?"
options.then: Dadi squeezes your hand. "Tell me your plan. I'll speak to him."

steps.why: Telling a trusted adult it's pressure gets you support. Marriage pressure is never your fault.

steps.prompt: A month later, Tauji asks: "So, what is this big plan of yours?"

options.text: "Nothing fixed yet, Tauji. I'll just see what happens after boards."
options.then: "Then we'll fix it for you," he says, smiling.

options.text: "Why? So you can find a flaw in it?"
options.then: He frowns. "I asked because I'm interested."

options.text: "Engineering, then a job. Marriage later, if and when I decide."
options.then: Tauji nods slowly. "Engineering. Your grandfather wanted that too."

options.text: "Ask Papa. He knows what I'm planning."
options.then: Tauji turns to Papa, and your plan becomes theirs to discuss.

steps.why: A clear plan, shared openly, shows the timeline is yours and well thought through.

scenarios.relearn: You can hear family out and still hold that whether and when are your call.

scenarios.hook: Your partner Dhruv has started saying that waiting means you don't care.
scenarios.setup: He brings it up again on the walk home.

steps.prompt: Dhruv says: "If you really cared, you wouldn't make me wait."

options.text: "If caring means that, maybe something's wrong with me."
options.then: He says, "No, no," but doesn't take back what he said.

options.text: "Caring doesn't come with a deadline. I'm not ready."
options.then: Dhruv kicks a pebble. "I didn't mean it like that."

options.text: "So you only care about one thing, then?"
options.then: "That's not fair," he snaps, and you walk the rest in silence.

options.text: "It's not about you. My parents would kill me."
options.then: "They don't have to know," he says, and the pressure just shifts.

steps.why: Caring and readiness are separate. Saying so plainly keeps your answer clear.

steps.prompt: The next day, Dhruv texts: "I just feel like you'd be ready if you loved me."

options.text: "Maybe you're right. I'll ask my friends what they think."
options.then: Dhruv replies fast: "Ask anyone. They'll tell you I'm right."

options.text: "Then maybe you need someone who loves you more."
options.then: "That's not what I said," he replies, stung.

options.text: "I'm sorry I'm making this so hard for you."
options.then: He says it's fine, and you carry guilt you didn't earn.

options.text: "Love and readiness are different. I'm sure of my no."
options.then: He takes a while to reply. "Okay. I hear you."

steps.why: Guilt isn't a reason. Your no stands, whatever the feelings.

steps.prompt: That evening, your grown-up sister Ruchi didi asks: "You've been quiet. Did something happen with Dhruv?"

options.text: "Nothing. All couples argue about this."
options.then: Ruchi nods, unsure, and you keep it to yourself.

options.text: "He says waiting means I don't care. It's weighing on me."
options.then: Ruchi puts her phone down. "That's guilt, not love. You've done nothing wrong."

options.text: "Do you think I'm being unfair to him?"
options.then: Ruchi frowns. "Unfair? For not being ready?"

options.text: "Can you find out if his friends think I'm cold?"
options.then: Ruchi raises an eyebrow. "Why does their view matter more than yours?"

steps.why: Sharing it with someone you trust helps. Pressure like this is never your fault.

scenarios.relearn: 'If you cared' is guilt, not a reason; caring doesn't override your readiness.

scenarios.hook: Your classmate Varun spots a contraception article open on your phone.
scenarios.setup: He calls the others over to look.

steps.prompt: Varun laughs and says: "Why are you reading that? That's so weird."

options.text: "It's for a project. I'm not actually interested."
options.then: "Sure it is," he grins, and the others laugh harder.

options.text: "Ugh, fine. I'll stop looking it up."
options.then: You close the tab, and your questions go with it.

options.text: "At least I'll know more than you ever will."
options.then: "Ooh," the group goes, and Varun's grin turns mean.

options.text: "Knowing my options is smart, not weird."
options.then: Varun shrugs. "I mean, fair. Is it any good?"

steps.why: Owning it plainly shows there's nothing strange about being informed.

steps.prompt: Varun asks: "Why do you even need to know? Are you planning something?"

options.text: "Mind your own business, Varun."
options.then: Varun rolls his eyes. "Touchy."

options.text: "No. Knowing the facts is useful, whatever I decide."
options.then: Varun thinks for a second. "Huh. Honestly, I've got questions too."

options.text: "Yeah, obviously. Jealous?"
options.then: The group whoops, and a rumour starts by lunch.

options.text: "No! I'm not like that. It just popped up on my feed, I swear."
options.then: Varun smirks. "Sure. Popped up." The teasing keeps going.

steps.why: Information helps every choice, including waiting. Reading up says nothing about your plans.

steps.prompt: Later, Varun asks quietly: "So where would someone even get real info?"

options.text: "Just search it. The first result is usually right."
options.then: He scrolls through ads and scary forum posts.

options.text: "Ask your older brother. He seems to know everything."
options.then: His brother laughs at him and hands him half-truths.

options.text: "An adolescent-friendly clinic or a doctor. It's confidential."
options.then: Varun nods. "Confidential? Okay. I might actually go."

options.text: "Why should I tell you after you laughed?"
options.then: Varun shrugs, embarrassed, and walks off still guessing.

steps.why: Pointing a friend to a confidential clinic gets them facts, not rumours.

scenarios.relearn: Seeking accurate information is the mature move, not something to be mocked for.

scenarios.hook: At a party, your partner Sahil pushes you to decide about going further.
scenarios.setup: He wants an answer this second.

steps.prompt: Sahil says: "Decide right now, or the moment's gone."

options.text: "Maybe the moment matters more than me being sure."
options.then: He takes your pause as a maybe, and the pressure in the room builds.

options.text: "Sorry. I'm ruining the night, aren't I?"
options.then: "You're not ruining anything," he says, "if you just say yes."

options.text: "A real choice isn't rushed. If it can't wait, it's no."
options.then: Sahil steps back. "Okay. Okay, no."

options.text: "Then go find someone else who'll say yes."
options.then: He looks hurt. "That's not what I meant."

steps.why: A choice that can't wait for you to be sure is already a no.

steps.prompt: Sahil asks: "Everyone else here is having fun. Why are you so serious?"

options.text: "Maybe I'm just too uptight for parties like this."
options.then: He laughs. "A little," and keeps pressing.

options.text: "Because this matters to me. My answer is still no."
options.then: Sahil goes quiet, then nods. "Fine. Let's go back to the others."

options.text: "Prove you're not just using me, then."
options.then: "How?" he asks, and the conversation tangles further.

options.text: "If I say no, will you still like me?"
options.then: "Of course," he says, but the pressure doesn't stop.

steps.why: Repeating your answer calmly keeps it clear. Taking it seriously isn't a flaw.

steps.prompt: The next day, your Mausi, whom you confide in, asks: "You seem shaken. Want to talk?"

options.text: "It's nothing. I probably led him on."
options.then: "Saying no isn't leading anyone on," Mausi says gently.

options.text: "Do you think I overreacted last night?"
options.then: Mausi shakes her head. "Wanting time is never overreacting."

options.text: "Sahil pushed me to decide fast. Can we talk about it?"
options.then: Mausi listens. "Pushing like that isn't okay. You did nothing wrong."

options.text: "It's private. Couples sort these things out."
options.then: Mausi nods, and the night stays tangled up inside you.

steps.why: Talking to a trusted adult helps you sort it out. Being pressured is never your fault.

scenarios.relearn: You can refuse a rushed deadline; a real choice isn't decided under pressure.

scenarios.hook: At the canteen, the group is mocking Zoya for choosing to wait, and she looks at you.
scenarios.setup: Someone turns to you for backup.

steps.prompt: Aditya asks: "Come on. You agree she's being a baby about it, right?"

options.text: "I mean, maybe she is a bit slow about it."
options.then: The laughter gets louder, and Zoya stares at her plate.

options.text: "No. Her pace is hers, and waiting is valid. Drop it."
options.then: Aditya rolls his eyes, but the table goes quiet, and Zoya exhales.

options.text: "I'm staying out of this one."
options.then: The teasing carries on, and Zoya stops looking at you.

options.text: "You're one to talk, Aditya. Nobody even likes you."
options.then: Aditya flares up, and now the fight is about you two.

steps.why: Saying it plainly backs her without turning it into a new fight.

steps.prompt: The next day the jokes start again, and Aditya asks: "What? It's just a joke. She knows we're kidding, right?"

options.text: "Fine, but maybe tone it down a bit."
options.then: He tones it down for a minute, then starts again.

options.text: "Okay, if she knows it's a joke, never mind."
options.then: Zoya picks up her tray and leaves.

options.text: "It stops being a joke when she's not laughing."
options.then: Aditya glances at Zoya's face and mutters, "Okay. Sorry."

options.text: "Joke about yourself, then, and see how it feels."
options.then: "Wow, okay," he says, and the table splits into sides.

steps.why: Pointing to how she actually feels shows the joke for what it is.

steps.prompt: After class, Zoya asks you quietly: "Do you think I'm weird for waiting?"

options.text: "Kind of, but it's your life."
options.then: Zoya nods slowly and goes quiet for the rest of the day.

options.text: "Honestly, just don't tell people next time."
options.then: Zoya frowns. "So it's something to hide?"

options.text: "Ignore them. They'll find someone else to tease soon enough."
options.then: Zoya shrugs. "Maybe," she says, still unsure about herself.

options.text: "Not at all. And if it keeps up, I'll go to a teacher with you."
options.then: Zoya smiles for the first time today. "Thanks. I'll tell you if it does."

steps.why: Backing her choice, and offering a trusted adult's help, answers her real worry.

scenarios.relearn: You can back a friend's right to wait; their pace is theirs and fully valid.

scenarios.hook: Karan, a family friend in his late twenties, keeps messaging you.
scenarios.setup: Tonight his message arrives after eleven.

steps.prompt: Karan writes: "You're mature for your age, so this is fine. Don't tell anyone."

options.text: "Thanks. I guess older people just get me better."
options.then: "Exactly," he replies, and asks to meet this weekend.

options.text: "No, this isn't okay. I'm telling a trusted adult."
options.then: He replies, "Relax, I was joking," then goes quiet.

options.text: "Our chats are private. It's no one else's business."
options.then: "Exactly. Our secret," he writes, and the messages keep coming.

options.text: "Maybe I'm just reading too much into this."
options.then: "You are," he writes. "We're just friends." The late messages continue.

steps.why: An adult asking for secrecy is a flag. Telling a trusted adult is always right.

steps.prompt: The next morning, your school counsellor, Mr. Reddy, asks: "You look tired. Everything okay?"

options.text: "It's my fault. I kept replying to him."
options.then: "Replying doesn't make any of this your fault," he says gently.

options.text: "A family friend messages me at night. It feels off."
options.then: Mr. Reddy sets down his pen. "Thank you for telling me. Let's talk."

options.text: "He's a family friend, so it's probably fine."
options.then: He pauses. "Family friends can cross lines too. What's happened?"

options.text: "It's private. Some things should stay in the family."
options.then: Mr. Reddy nods. "That's okay. Will you sit with me for a few minutes anyway?"

steps.why: Naming what feels off to a trusted adult is how you get protected. It's never your fault.

steps.prompt: Later that day, Mr. Reddy says: "If anyone makes you uneasy, we can call Childline 1098 together. Would that be okay?"

options.text: "Isn't Childline only for little kids?"
options.then: "It's for anyone under 18," he says. "That includes you."

options.text: "Yes. I'd feel safer with you there."
options.then: Mr. Reddy dials, stays beside you, and the person on the line listens.

options.text: "I'll confront him first, so he knows I'm not scared."
options.then: "Please don't face him alone," he says. "Let's keep you safe first."

options.text: "If he gets in trouble, it's my fault."
options.then: "What he did is on him, not you," Mr. Reddy says.

steps.why: Childline 1098 and a trusted adult together can keep you safe.

steps.prompt: A week later, Mr. Reddy asks: "What would help you most from here?"

options.text: "I'll message Karan once and tell him off properly."
options.then: "Please don't contact him," he says. "Let the adults deal with him."

options.text: "Keep checking in with me, and help me tell my parents."
options.then: "Of course. Every week, and we'll talk to them together."

options.text: "I'll delete all his chats so I can stop thinking about it."
options.then: "Keep them for now," he says gently. "They can help keep you safe."

options.text: "Just check in if he messages again. Otherwise I'm fine."
options.then: "Let's check in anyway," he says. "How you feel matters too."

steps.why: Ongoing support and the adults around you keep you safe. None of this was your fault.

scenarios.relearn: An older person asking for secrecy is a flag; step back and tell a trusted adult.

scenarios.hook: Your girlfriend Pooja keeps hinting you're 'behind' because you're not ready.

steps.prompt: She jokes about it again in front of her friends. What do you do?

options.text: Search online for why you're 'behind' for your age
options.then: The search leaves you comparing yourself to strangers and feeling worse.

options.text: Tell her privately that your pace is yours, not 'behind'
options.then: Pooja looks surprised. "I didn't think it bothered you that much."

options.text: Tell her friends she's the one with the problem
options.then: Her friends go quiet, and Pooja is hurt and angry all evening.

options.text: Ask your friend Imran, who says to stop overthinking it
options.then: Imran shrugs. "Everyone's doing it." Now the pressure comes from two sides.

steps.why: Naming the label in private shows it's pressure, not a fact, without a public fight.

steps.prompt: A few days later, Pooja says she worries you don't find her attractive. What do you do?

options.text: Promise you'll be ready soon so she stops worrying
options.then: She smiles, and now there's a deadline in your head you never chose.

options.text: Tell her she's being dramatic about nothing
options.then: Her face falls, and she stops talking about it, still hurt.

options.text: Say you do, and that readiness is a separate thing
options.then: Pooja exhales. "Okay. I think I mixed the two up."

options.text: Apologise, feeling guilty for not being ready
options.then: She says it's fine, and you leave feeling like you did something wrong.

steps.why: Keeping attraction and readiness separate answers her worry honestly.

steps.prompt: The next week, your grown-up cousin Kiran didi asks how things are with Pooja. What do you say?

options.text: Say it's all perfect, since your love life is private
options.then: Kiran nods, and you carry the weight of it on your own.

options.text: Ask how to get ready faster so Pooja is happy
options.then: Kiran frowns. "Ready faster? Who's setting that clock?"

options.text: Tell her honestly about the 'behind' comments
options.then: Kiran listens. "Your pace is yours. Anyone who cares should get that."

options.text: Joke that you're the slow one, so it's no big deal
options.then: Kiran laughs, and the comments that bother you stay unspoken.

steps.why: Talking to someone you trust helps you hold your pace. Feeling pressured is never your fault.

scenarios.debrief: Readiness is personal; 'everyone's ahead' is pressure, not a deadline.
scenarios.relearn: Decide by your own readiness; 'you're behind' is a push, not a fact.

scenarios.hook: Kunal asked you out, and now the whole class is gossiping about your answer.

steps.prompt: You're about to say yes mainly so the gossip stops. What do you do?

options.text: Say yes tonight. The gossip will die down after that
options.then: The gossip stops for a day, then turns to guessing how long you'll last.

options.text: Pause and ask yourself whether you actually want this
options.then: Sitting with it, you realise you're not sure yet, and that's okay.

options.text: Say no fast, just to prove the gossips wrong
options.then: The gossip switches to why you said no, and you're still unsure.

options.text: Ask the class group chat to vote on it
options.then: The chat explodes with votes, and Kunal sees all of it.

steps.why: A choice made to quiet others isn't really yours. Pausing gives it back to you.

steps.prompt: The next day, a friend says choices like this should be about what earns you respect. What do you think?

options.text: She's right. Reputation matters most at our age
options.then: You start replaying what everyone might think, and lose track of what you feel.

options.text: It should come from what I want, not who's watching
options.then: Your friend shrugs. "Fair. It's your life."

options.text: Whatever ends the gossip fastest is the right call
options.then: The gossip is the only thing you're thinking about now.

options.text: I'd ask my older sister what people will say
options.then: Your sister tells you what people will say, but not what you want.

steps.why: Respect from others is no basis for a choice that is yours to live with.

steps.prompt: A week later, Kunal asks how you honestly feel about him. What do you do?

options.text: Tell him what your friends think of him
options.then: Kunal looks confused. "I asked about you, not them."

options.text: Say you're crazy about him, to skip an awkward talk
options.then: Kunal beams, and you feel further from the truth than before.

options.text: Say whatever will keep the class quiet
options.then: Kunal can tell something's off, and the gossip keeps going anyway.

options.text: Tell him honestly where you are, even if it's unsure
options.then: Kunal nods. "Thanks for being straight with me."

steps.why: An honest answer, even an unsure one, is the only one that's truly yours.

scenarios.debrief: If you're choosing mainly to please or quiet others, pause and reclaim it.
scenarios.relearn: If a choice is mainly to please others, pause and re-decide from your values.

scenarios.hook: After your Class 12 results, your parents start talking about finding you a match.

steps.prompt: At dinner, Papa says a good family has asked about you. What do you do?

options.text: Believe a good daughter shouldn't have plans of her own
options.then: Papa takes it as a yes and mentions a meeting.

options.text: Say calmly that you want to study first, and ask to talk
options.then: Papa sets down his spoon. "Talk, then. We're listening."

options.text: Shout that they only care about getting rid of you
options.then: Mummy's eyes fill up. "How can you say that to us?"

options.text: Ask your cousin, who says it's easier to go along
options.then: Your cousin shrugs. "Everyone adjusts." You feel more alone.

steps.why: Saying your plan calmly opens a real conversation about your own future.

steps.prompt: Mummy says marriage won't stop you studying later. What do you say?

options.text: Believe her, since plenty of girls study after marriage
options.then: Mummy smiles, and the meeting with the family gets a date.

options.text: Say she married young, and look how that turned out
options.then: Mummy goes silent, and the hurt hangs over the house for days.

options.text: Say you'd like to decide on marriage after your degree
options.then: Mummy pauses. "After your degree." She looks thoughtful.

options.text: Ask them to wait just until your first-year exams
options.then: Papa agrees. "First year, then we look." The deadline has only moved.

steps.why: Naming your own timing keeps whether and when with you.

steps.prompt: The next day, your teacher Ms. Iyer notices you look worried. What do you do?

options.text: Believe family matters should never leave the house
options.then: Ms. Iyer says her door is always open, and the worry follows you home.

options.text: Ask her to call your parents and tell them off
options.then: She shakes her head gently. "Let's not start a fight. Tell me more first."

options.text: Tell her about the marriage talk and ask for her help
options.then: Ms. Iyer listens, then says, "You're not alone in this. Let's plan."

options.text: Ask her whether wanting college makes you selfish
options.then: "Not at all," she says. "Wanting to study isn't selfish."

steps.why: A trusted adult can stand with you. Pressure to marry is never your fault.

steps.prompt: A week later, the school invites parents in to talk about college plans. What do you do?

options.text: Skip it and let the adults decide between them
options.then: The adults talk politely, and nothing gets decided about you.

options.text: Ask to join the meeting and share your plan yourself
options.then: In the meeting, Papa asks you real questions about courses.

options.text: Hope the teachers make your case without you
options.then: A teacher speaks up, but Papa asks why you didn't say it yourself.

options.text: Leave a list of colleges on their table and stay out of it
options.then: The list sits untouched, and the adults meet without you.

steps.why: Speaking for your own future, with a trusted adult beside you, carries the most weight.

steps.prompt: That evening, Papa asks if you'll still listen to your parents as you grow up. What do you say?

options.text: Apologise for causing so much worry at home
options.then: Papa softens, but the question of a match stays open.

options.text: Say you'd rather not get into this tonight
options.then: Papa frowns. "We need to talk about it sometime, beta."

options.text: Say they never listen to you, so why should you
options.then: Papa sighs and leaves the table without another word.

options.text: Say you'll always listen, and the choice will still be yours
options.then: Papa nods slowly. "Listening is all we ask. Study well."

steps.why: Valuing their voice while keeping the decision yours respects everyone.

scenarios.debrief: You can value family and keep your timeline. Marriage pressure is never your fault: if it continues, tell a trusted adult or call Childline 1098.
scenarios.relearn: You can respect family input while holding whether and when as your choice.

scenarios.hook: In your class group chat, people are mocking Ishaan for choosing to wait.

options.text: Stay quiet so the group doesn't turn on you

options.text: Post a joke to change the topic without taking sides

steps.prompt: The next day, Ishaan messages to ask if everyone was laughing at him. What do you reply?

options.text: Tell him no one really cares, so forget it

options.text: Tell him he shouldn't have shared it in the first place

options.text: Mute the chat. You've done your part already

scenarios.debrief: Standing up for a friend's pace protects everyone's right to choose freely.

options.then: Guilt creeps in, though you've done nothing wrong.

options.text: Tell him you won't decide under a deadline

options.text: Ask your friend Ritu, who says just say yes and see

options.text: Tell him he's being manipulative and childish

steps.prompt: That weekend, your grown-up cousin Leela didi asks why you seem tense. What do you do?

options.text: Say it's nothing, since couples sort out their own fights
options.then: Leela lets it go, and you're left untangling it alone.

options.text: Ask her how to make Sameer stop being upset
options.then: Leela frowns. "Why is his mood your job to fix?"

options.text: Laugh it off. Every relationship has some drama

options.text: Tell her about the deadlines and ask what she thinks
options.then: Leela listens. "Deadlines like that are pressure. Your pace counts."

options.text: Tell his friends so they talk some sense into him

options.text: Tell him you'll decide in your own time, deadline or not

scenarios.debrief: Manufactured urgency is pressure, never your fault. You can always take the time you need.
scenarios.relearn: 'Decide now or never' is a tactic; a real choice isn't rushed.

scenarios.hook: You have a sexual health question, but asking a clinic feels immature.

options.text: Skip it and piece it together from rumours

options.text: Wait until you can ask without anyone ever knowing

options.text: Ask anyway. Getting the facts is the grown-up move
options.then: You book a slot at the adolescent-friendly clinic for Saturday.

options.text: Sign up for a private chat and ask your question

options.text: Skip it, since others might see you sign up
options.then: You watch students go in one by one, not knowing the chats are confidential.

options.text: Ask it out loud in the talk, as a joke
options.then: The class laughs, and the counsellor's serious answer gets lost.

steps.why: Asking directly, in private, gets you the real answer for your own choice.

steps.prompt: Later, your friend Kabir jokes that only kids ask counsellors things. What do you say?

options.then: Kabir moves on, and you feel oddly small for hiding it.

scenarios.debrief: Seeking accurate information from a clinic, with a trusted adult's guidance if you like, is exactly what maturity looks like.

options.text: Tell yourself it's flattering, so maybe it's fine

options.text: Ask your friends if older guys liking you is normal

steps.prompt: Vikram asks to meet alone and says no one needs to know. What do you do?

options.then: Tara relaxes, and now you both hold a secret that feels heavy.

options.then: Tara's eyes fill. "You'd come with me? Okay."

scenarios.debrief: This is a flag, never your fault. Tell a trusted adult or call Childline 1098.
scenarios.relearn: Older-person pressure plus 'keep it secret' is a flag; step back and tell someone.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a choice that's truly yours, or one that's really someone else's?

scenarios.hook: "Once you've agreed once, you can't change your mind later."

scenarios.hook: "If you're on the pill, you don't need condoms for anything."

myth.un: On the pill, you never need condoms.
myth.re: The pill prevents pregnancy only; a condom is still what protects against STIs.
myth.why: Each method does a different job.

scenarios.relearn: The pill covers pregnancy; only condoms add STI protection. That's why people pair them.

scenarios.hook: "The emergency pill only works the next morning, then it's useless."

myth.un: EC only works the very next morning.
myth.re: It works best within 5 days of unprotected sex. Sooner is better, but it isn't only for the morning after.
myth.why: It mainly works by delaying ovulation.

scenarios.relearn: EC has a 5-day window; act sooner for the best chance, but the morning after isn't the only moment.

scenarios.hook: "You can't get contraception unless you're married."

myth.un: Only married people can get contraception.
myth.re: Condoms and the EC pill are sold at any pharmacy, and AFHC (Ujala) clinics give confidential information to young people.
myth.why: Access isn't tied to marital status.

scenarios.relearn: A pharmacy sells condoms/EC to anyone; AFHC clinics inform young people confidentially.

scenarios.hook: "An IUD will leave you unable to have children later."

myth.un: An IUD leaves you unable to have children later.
myth.re: The IUD is reversible. Once removed, fertility returns; it doesn't cause later infertility.
myth.why: It prevents pregnancy only while it's in place.

scenarios.relearn: LARC like the IUD is reversible; fertility returns after it's removed.

scenarios.hook: "You can't get pregnant the very first time."

myth.un: You can't get pregnant the first time.
myth.re: Any unprotected sex can lead to pregnancy or an STI, including the first time.
myth.why: The body doesn't keep count of 'firsts'.

scenarios.relearn: There's no 'free pass' first time; it's the act, not the count, that carries risk.

scenarios.hook: "Pulling out in time is as good as a condom."

myth.un: Pulling out is as good as a condom.
myth.re: Withdrawal is far less reliable and gives no STI protection; a condom does both jobs better.
myth.why: It depends on perfect timing and covers no STIs.

scenarios.relearn: Withdrawal is unreliable and STI-blind; a condom is the more dependable, dual-protection choice.

scenarios.hook: "A safe day on the calendar means you never need protection."

myth.un: A 'safe day' means you never need protection.
myth.re: Cycle timing is hard to predict, so a 'safe day' guess is unreliable; protection is what actually covers you.
myth.why: Ovulation timing shifts and can't be guessed exactly.

scenarios.relearn: 'Safe day' guessing is unreliable; a real method is what protects you.

scenarios.hook: "Condoms fail so often there's no point using them."

myth.un: Condoms fail so often there's no point.
myth.re: Used correctly every time they're highly effective, about 98 in 100, and they're the only STI protection.
myth.why: Most 'failure' is inconsistent or incorrect use.

scenarios.relearn: Used right every time, condoms work well and uniquely guard against STIs.

scenarios.hook: "The implant has to be taken out and put back every month."

myth.un: The implant is swapped every month.
myth.re: The implant is long-acting. Once fitted it lasts a few years with nothing to do daily.
myth.why: That's the whole point of LARC.

scenarios.relearn: LARC like the implant lasts years; there's nothing monthly or daily to remember.

scenarios.hook: "Taking the emergency pill is basically having an abortion."

myth.un: The emergency pill is basically an abortion.
myth.re: EC prevents pregnancy, mainly by delaying ovulation; it cannot end an existing pregnancy.
myth.why: Prevention after sex is not termination.

scenarios.relearn: EC prevents pregnancy and is not an abortion; the two are different things.

scenarios.hook: "Choosing not to have sex isn't a real form of protection."

myth.un: Not having sex isn't real protection.
myth.re: Delaying / not having sex is the only 100%-certain option against pregnancy and STIs, and it's fully valid.
myth.why: No exposure means no risk.

scenarios.relearn: Delaying is the most certain option and an equal, respected choice, never a lesser one.

scenarios.hook: "Two condoms at once give you double the protection."

myth.un: Two condoms give double protection.
myth.re: Doubling up causes friction and is more likely to tear; one condom used correctly is the protective choice.
myth.why: More isn't safer here. Correct single use is.

scenarios.relearn: One condom, used right, protects best; doubling up backfires.

scenarios.hook: "Protection talk is only for people who could get pregnant."

myth.un: Protection only matters if pregnancy is possible.
myth.re: STI protection matters for any partners; condoms and check-ups are part of looking after each other's health.
myth.why: Health, not just pregnancy, is the point.

scenarios.relearn: Protection is about health for everyone, not only about pregnancy.

scenarios.hook: "Knowing about contraception just pushes young people into sex."

myth.un: Knowing about contraception pushes you into sex.
myth.re: Good information helps people make safer, more thoughtful choices, including choosing to wait.
myth.why: Knowledge informs a choice; it doesn't make it.

scenarios.relearn: Information empowers a free choice, including delaying. It doesn't nudge anyone anywhere.

scenarios.hook: "You can flush out pregnancy risk by washing right after sex."

myth.un: Washing after sex prevents pregnancy.
myth.re: Washing does nothing to prevent pregnancy; a real method or the EC pill is what works.
myth.why: It can't reach or stop what's already happened.

scenarios.relearn: Washing isn't contraception; a real method beforehand or EC afterward is what protects you.

scenarios.hook: "Starting the pill young will mess up your fertility for good."

myth.un: The pill young ruins your fertility.
myth.re: The pill is reversible; fertility returns after you stop, whatever age you started.
myth.why: It prevents pregnancy while taken, not after.

scenarios.relearn: The pill is reversible at any age you start; stopping returns your fertility.

scenarios.hook: You and Leena are working out a protection plan together.
scenarios.setup: You're sharing a plate of momos after class.

steps.prompt: Leena asks: "So what do you actually want, if we ever get there?"

options.text: "If we ever do, I want us to use a condom. Agreed?"
options.then: Leena nods. "Agreed. I was hoping you'd say that."

options.text: "I guess we'll just figure it out in the moment."
options.then: "In the moment?" she says. "That sounds stressful."

options.text: "Whatever you want. I don't mind."
options.then: "I asked what you want," Leena says, laughing.

options.text: "Don't worry. I'll handle all of that."
options.then: "I'd like a say too," Leena says, frowning a little.

steps.why: Saying clearly what you want, ahead of time, makes it a real agreement.

steps.prompt: Leena asks: "Is a condom enough, or should we use something else too?"

options.text: "A condom's useless. Let's just use the pill."
options.then: "Useless?" Leena asks. "Then what about STIs?"

options.text: "It's enough. Nothing ever goes wrong with them."
options.then: "Never?" Leena asks. "I read they can slip."

options.text: "It covers STIs. Let's ask a clinic about adding more."
options.then: Leena smiles. "Okay. Let's go together."

options.text: "Let's ask your friends what they use."
options.then: "They'll all say different things," Leena sighs.

steps.why: Condoms protect against STIs, and a clinic can explain extra pregnancy cover.

steps.prompt: Leena asks: "And if one of us changes our mind about any of this?"

options.text: "We've agreed. No changing it now."
options.then: Leena frowns. "Even if something feels wrong?"

options.text: "Then we say so, and the other one listens."
options.then: "Deal," Leena says, and taps her cup against yours.

options.text: "Then I guess we'd just break up."
options.then: Leena stares at you. "Over that?"

options.text: "Then we go with whoever feels more strongly."
options.then: "That could leave one of us unhappy," Leena says.

steps.why: Agreements work when either of you can speak up and be heard.

scenarios.relearn: Protection is something partners agree on together, clearly and ahead of time.

options.then: Two methods stand out once you see what really fits you.

steps.why: Your own needs and values are what make a method fit.

steps.prompt: Priya teases you for taking so long to decide. What do you do?

options.text: Take the time you need. It's your choice
options.then: Priya shrugs and agrees that it's your call.

options.text: Pick her method so she drops it
options.then: The teasing stops, and you're left with a choice that isn't yours.

options.text: Decide today, just to end the teasing
options.then: You decide in a rush, and the doubt arrives that night.

options.text: Stop talking to Priya about anything personal
options.then: Priya feels hurt, and you lose a friend's support too.

steps.why: A real choice isn't rushed. Take the time you need.

scenarios.debrief: Gather the facts and weigh your own needs. The choice is yours.
scenarios.relearn: There's no single 'right' method; the right one fits your needs.

scenarios.hook: You're not sure you're ready for sex, but your friends keep saying it's time.

steps.prompt: At lunch, they tease you about still waiting. What goes through your mind?

options.text: Maybe something's wrong with me for waiting
options.then: The worry follows you home and keeps you up that night.

options.text: Waiting is valid, and my timing is mine
options.then: The teasing still stings, but you feel steadier about your own pace.

options.text: I should decide this week, to end the teasing
options.then: A deadline appears in your head that nobody actually set.

options.text: Maybe they know better, since they're older
options.then: You start trusting their timeline more than your own.

steps.why: Waiting is common and respected. Nothing is wrong with you for waiting.

steps.prompt: Your partner Aman asks when you think you'll be ready. What do you say?

options.text: That you'll be ready soon, so he isn't hurt
options.then: Aman brightens, and you feel a timer start ticking.

options.text: That your friends think you should be by now
options.then: Aman asks what you think, and you realise you haven't said.

options.text: That you don't know yet, and that's okay
options.then: Aman nods and says he'll wait until you're sure.

options.text: That he should stop asking or you'll break up
options.then: Aman looks stung, and the talk ends in silence.

steps.why: You don't owe anyone a date. Readiness is yours to decide.

steps.prompt: A week later, a friend says waiting means you're a prude. What do you do?

options.text: Ask an older cousin, who says to just get it over with
options.then: The advice adds one more voice that isn't yours.

options.text: Snap back that she's the one with a problem
options.then: She snaps back, and the lunch table goes quiet.

options.text: Wonder if she's right and you're too uptight
options.then: The word 'prude' stays with you for days.

options.text: Say waiting is your choice, and leave it there
options.then: She shrugs, and the talk moves on to other things.

steps.why: Waiting isn't prudish. It's a common, respected choice.

steps.prompt: The pressure keeps building. Who do you talk to about it?

options.text: An adult you trust, like your aunt or a counsellor
options.then: Your aunt listens and reminds you the timing is yours alone.

options.text: The same friends who keep teasing you
options.then: They laugh it off, and you feel more alone.

options.text: An online forum full of strangers
options.then: Strangers give loud opinions that don't fit your life.

options.text: Aman, and ask him to make the decision for you
options.then: Aman hesitates, unsure it should be his call.

steps.why: Pressure is never your fault, and someone you trust can help you keep your own pace.

scenarios.debrief: Waiting is a full, equal option, and no one should pressure you.
scenarios.relearn: Delaying is respected and the most certain choice; the timing is yours.

scenarios.hook: Your friend Swati asks what the emergency pill actually does.

steps.prompt: She's heard three different things. What do you tell her?

options.text: It ends a pregnancy that has already begun
options.then: Swati repeats it to two friends, and the myth spreads.

options.text: It stops a pregnancy starting. It's not an abortion
options.then: Swati looks relieved. She'd thought it was something else.

options.text: It's a daily pill, the same as the regular one
options.then: Swati thinks it's a regular method and plans around that.

options.text: It protects against STIs as well as pregnancy
options.then: Swati thinks she's covered for infections, though she isn't.

steps.why: EC prevents pregnancy, mainly by delaying ovulation. It can't end a pregnancy.

steps.prompt: Swati asks how soon it has to be taken. What do you say?

options.text: Any time within a month, so there's no rush
options.then: Swati relaxes, thinking she has weeks to decide.

options.text: Only the next morning. After that, it's useless
options.then: Swati thinks the chance is gone after one day.

options.text: As soon as possible. It works best within 5 days
options.then: Swati notes it down: sooner is better, within 5 days.

options.text: Whenever she gets round to it
options.then: Swati shrugs, and the timing stays fuzzy.

steps.why: EC works best the sooner it's taken, within 5 days.

steps.prompt: Swati asks where someone could get it. What do you tell her?

options.text: Only a hospital, after a long wait in a queue
options.then: Swati frowns. "Then it might be too late by the time you're seen."

options.text: A clinic or doctor. A trusted adult can help too
options.then: Swati nods. "So there's real help, and she needn't go alone."

options.text: Online, from whoever is cheapest
options.then: Swati worries about fakes and late deliveries.

options.text: From a friend's older sister, who might have some
options.then: Swati feels awkward asking someone else's sister for medicine.

steps.why: A doctor or clinic gives EC advice privately, and a trusted adult can help someone get there.

steps.prompt: Swati asks if someone could just use it instead of a regular method. What do you say?

options.text: Yes, if they only need it now and then
options.then: Swati files it away as a regular option.

options.text: No. It's a backup, not a regular method
options.then: Swati nods. "So it's for when something goes wrong."

options.text: Yes. It's simpler than remembering a daily pill
options.then: Swati thinks that sounds easier than the pill.

options.text: Only if their partner agrees to it
options.then: Swati frowns, unsure what the partner has to do with it.

steps.why: EC is a backup for when something goes wrong, not an everyday method.

scenarios.debrief: EC prevents pregnancy, best within 5 days, and is not an abortion.
scenarios.relearn: EC is a time-limited backup that prevents pregnancy.

scenarios.hook: A class WhatsApp group swears that on a 'safe day', you don't need protection.

steps.prompt: Your friend Nisha asks if it's true. What do you tell her?

options.text: It's probably true, since so many people say it
options.then: Nisha starts to believe it, and so do two others she tells.

options.text: Safe days are guesses. A real method protects you
options.then: Nisha frowns, surprised the whole group could be wrong.

options.text: Forward it to your cousins, in case it helps
options.then: The forward reaches your cousins, and one of them believes it.

options.text: No idea. Ask the group admin
options.then: The admin replies with a laughing face and nothing else.

steps.why: Cycle timing can't be reliably guessed. A real method protects you.

steps.prompt: Someone in the group replies that it 'worked for her sister'. What do you do?

options.text: Point out that luck isn't the same as a method
options.then: A few people react with a thumbs up, and the thread goes quiet.

options.text: Accept it, since a real person tried it
options.then: The myth gains another believer, and the forwards continue.

options.text: Call her out by name in front of everyone
options.then: The thread turns into an argument, and nobody discusses facts.

options.text: Leave the group without saying anything
options.then: The myth keeps spreading, though you're no longer there to see it.

steps.why: One person's luck doesn't make a method reliable.

steps.prompt: Nisha asks where to get facts she can actually trust. What do you suggest?

options.text: The most popular health influencer online
options.then: The video is slick, and half of it is wrong.

options.text: The aunty in the family group who knows everything
options.then: The aunty sends three more forwards, each one a myth.

options.text: A doctor, a pharmacist or an adolescent clinic
options.then: Nisha books a visit to the clinic near her school.

options.text: Whatever most of the class believes
options.then: The class splits into camps, and the myth survives.

steps.why: Doctors and clinics give facts, not forwards.

steps.prompt: Nisha wants to post one calm reply to the group. What should it say?

options.text: Some say it works and some don't. Your call
options.then: A few people read it as permission to keep guessing.

options.text: Safe days are a lie, and you're all idiots
options.then: The group gets defensive, and nobody listens after that.

options.text: Safe days can't be guessed. Ask a doctor or clinic
options.then: A couple of people reply asking where the clinic is.

options.text: Safe days will ruin your life. Don't risk anything
options.then: The scary tone puts people off, and the forward keeps circulating.

steps.why: A calm, factual reply helps others without shaming anyone.

scenarios.debrief: 'Safe day' guessing is unreliable. Trust a method, not a forward.
scenarios.relearn: Cycle timing can't be guessed; a real method protects you.
